utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. We have not sort of formally set out time limits for today's proceedings. I would imagine that it would be fair to say the Defence would have this session to make its submissions; most probably the Prosecution might make its response in the next session; and if there is any reply, it will be in the third session. Would that be okay by everybody? Would it be okay with you, Mr. Milovancevic? You are the one to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hope one session will suffice for oral submissions. Perhaps there might be a need for a small portion of the next session, but that will largely depend on my pace and we shouldn't forget the interpretation, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Do you have anything to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Obviously it depends on what submissions are made by the Defence and how long it's going to take us to respond to them and in what detail and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. At this moment the Defence, according to Rule 98 bis, needs to put forward oral submissions, after which the Chamber will be able to potentially acquit our client, should the Chamber establish that there are no foundations for the indictment in place. And the Defence intends to do that in the following oral submissions. At the very beginning, we wish to state that in these proceedings so far, against the accused, Milan Martic, the OTP has not proven or even made it possible to further corroborate the allegations from their indictment. At this moment the Defence is of the view that there is no evidence against the accused, Martic, and we expect the Chamber to acquit the accused on all counts. At the beginning of our oral submissions, we wanted to mention one thing. How was it possible that even before we submit our submissions and before we hear the arguments of the OTP and before the Chamber has ruled on it, that the Chamber issued a decision on the continuation of the proceedings? Does that mean -- is this prejudicial to the Defence? We also believe that the Defence suffered from another thing that may have happened, and that was concerning the basic factual allegations after we've heard the case of the Prosecutor, by such an order by the Chamber on the continuation of the proceedings before we have submitted our oral submissions; this went to the detriment of the Defence. Another important issue needs to be raised, and we see no solution for that issue at this moment in the proceedings that would be in keeping with the interests of justice. The status of evidence of Witness Milan Babic remains unresolved. We have the Chamber's decision, which we may appeal against, and the rule on the admission of his evidence is not final -- the ruling is not final yet. Therefore, in such a situation, we ask: How is it possible for the Defence to continue working and presenting its case and what is it that we have before us or we do not have before us on the one hand? On the other hand, having in mind the unresolved situation with Mr. Babic, how can the Chamber decide on the Rule 98 bis in this case? Since we find ourselves in such a factual and legal situation, the Defence, in spite of all the problems, finds it in its interest and in the -- it is in the interest of the accused, Milan Martic, to put forth these oral submissions as to what has been proven in the previous phase of the proceedings and what has not and what is the position of the Defence concerning the legal position, as well as the allegations stipulated in the indictment put forward by our learned friends from the OTP. For one to be able to see what the position of Defence is, we need to start with the basic allegations of the indictment from paragraph 4 of the indictment, mentioning the purpose and the aim of the joint criminal enterprise. In paragraph 3 of the indictment, the OTP states that Milan Martic is held responsible for his participation in the joint criminal enterprise, and furthermore they state that the purpose of this joint criminal enterprise was the forcible removal of a majority of the non-Serb populations, being Croat and Muslim populations, from approximately one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia and large parts of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in order - and this is the joint criminal enterprise explained by the OTP - to make them part of a new Serb-dominated state. In paragraph 4, the Prosecutor defines those territories, stating that these are the territories of the SAO Krajina, the SAO Western Slavonia, the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, the area of the Dubrovnik republic, although such a name does not exist ins history, as well as the city of Zagreb. Therefore, in addition to the territory of Krajina, the goal of the joint criminal enterprise to include all those territories protected by the UN as well as the territory of the so-called -- the Dubrovnik republic and the city of Zagreb to be put under Serb domination within a single state. Not one of the paragraphs of the indictment make it clear as to who, when, where, how, and why made this plan of the joint criminal enterprise. We can't see whether that plan was done covertly or openly. Another thing that is not alleged, and it wasn't corroborated by any evidence by the OTP, was as to whether that was an oral or a written plan. The only thing alleged by the OTP is to be found in paragraph 6, and that is that the so-called joint criminal enterprise - and it is a so-called enterprise because we don't know who, when, where or how or by whom. Therefore, the Prosecutor in paragraph 6 stipulates that the perpetrators of the plan are the accused, Milan Martic; Slobodan Milosevic, the former Serbian president who has recently died and who was the main person in the plan; and on top of that, an entire spectrum of other people mentioned in paragraph 6, including Borislav Jovic, one of the members of the Presidency of Yugoslavia; and the president of the State Commission of Yugoslavia for Cooperation with UNPROFOR throughout the relevant time in the indictment; as well as Veljko Kadijevic, who was the federal secretary for national against, who was an army general; as well as General Blagoje Adzic, who was chief of the general staff of the armed forces of the SFRY. It is a well-known fact that Mr. Adzic and Kadijevic, 15 years after the commencement of the so-called joint criminal enterprise, have not been indicted by any single indictment at this Tribunal. They will never be tried, and I am not saying this because I think they should be. There is no basis for them to be indicted, and we've heard Mr. Theunens', the military expert of the OTP, who analysed in detail the constitutional regulation and the federal regulation of Yugoslavia, as well as all other relevant legal material, showed that the activities of the armed forces were regular in the then-territory of Yugoslavia under the command of those who had been authorised to command such armed forces and controlled by civilian authorities. That's why we do not have such an indictment in place. That's why it is absurd that Martic is being charged or indicted for commanding over the JNA forces and other forces that allegedly participated in the joint criminal enterprise; and yet at the same time, we don't have the people who truly commanded the armed forces of Yugoslavia, the JNA. This points to the basic problem of the Prosecutor's fictitious tale of the joint criminal enterprise. The hypothesis by the Prosecutor on the joint criminal enterprise, with the goal and purpose that we have mentioned already, is totally fictional and that has been proven through their own witnesses, a highly positioned official of the UN who holds a Ph.D. in science, Mr. Charles Kirudja was one of the OTP's witnesses. Mr. Kirudja was a highly positioned official of the UN, and he had been that before he came to Yugoslavia and he still is a highly positioned official of the UN. It is -- he's a well-educated person, he's knowledgeable; and based on that, he could provide relevant testimony as an OTP witness before this Tribunal. Mr. Kirudja managed to destroy the thesis of the -- the hypothesis of the joint criminal enterprise. He's explained that Mr. Milosevic, as the alleged creator of this infamous joint criminal enterprise, wanted to see Krajina with a large degree of autonomy as a part of the Republic of Croatia, whereas the OTP claims that the goal of the enterprise was to extract Krajina from Croatia and join it with Serbia. The president, the then-president, was of a completely different view according to the statement of Mr. Charles Kirudja, the OTP witness. He also testified that Milosevic, as the alleged head person of the enterprise, always sought a peaceful solution for Yugoslavia and that he kept telling him, as a UN official, that the situation in the Krajina and in Bosnia could not be resolved by the use of arms, which is completely contrary to the stipulations in the indictment. Mr. Kirudja, under oath, explained that Mr. Milosevic together with General Kadijevic, who was the then-federal secretary of national defence on the 23rd of November, 1991, in Geneva signed an agreement foreseeing the cessation of hostilities, the deblocking of the blocked JNA barracks, and the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia. This was the person who, according to the OTP, was the person who put together the devilish plan to remove that part of territory from Croatia and join it with Serbia. It was in November 1991 that Mr. Kirudja concluded this agreement, even before the UN deployment there, including a paragraph on the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia. Mr. Kirudja also testified that Mr. Milosevic supported the resolution of the UN called the Vance Plan, which established the peacekeeping operation of the UN in Yugoslavia. I wish to remind you, Your Honours, that this was a peacekeeping UN operation in Yugoslavia, not in Croatia, according to the Security Council's resolution. Mr. Kirudja, as an OTP witness and a high official of the UN stated that Mr. Milosevic supported the resolution, that he supported the leadership of Krajina, which in turn accepted the UN plan, as well as he mentioned Mr. Paspalj and other people from the Krajina. And he stated that Mr. Milosevic commented on Mr. Babic's behaviour in the media as being the only person who was against the deployment of the peacekeeping troops. During his testimony, the Defence put two documents before the Chamber, sent to the Security Council, signed by Mr. Milan Babic. We can see from those that he, as the president of the SAO Krajina in February 1992, states to the Secretary-General that he cannot accept the peacekeeping mission as envisaged and that the Assembly of Krajina had no authority to adopt such a plan, and that therefore the decision was an irregular and illegal one. Doesn't it strike you as ironic that the only witness who opposed the deployment of the peacekeeping forces in Yugoslavia, as confirmed by Mr. Kirudja, that that particular witness was put forth by the OTP to support their hypothesis that Milosevic was for war and that Babic, in turn, wanted something completely different? Logically speaking, it doesn't add up; factually, even worse or even less. Mr. Kirudja confirmed that, as a high official of the UN, he came to Yugoslavia in April. He stated that he met General Spiro Nikovic, who was the commander of the 10th Corps, and he confirmed that the general, as an honourable officer, a very senior officer of the JNA, stated that -- General Nikovic stated that the JNA supports the plan put forth, and that that includes Mr. Milosevic as well as the Presidency and the Federal Secretariat of National Defence. And that included the people from Krajina, including Mr. Babic, who were in support of such a plan. General Spiro Nikovic, according to Mr. Kirudja's words, told him that the JNA will hand over the territory to the UN and that the JNA will be withdrawing its forces in full from that area. Mr. Kirudja stated that General Nikovic had plans made on the withdrawal of the JNA from the area that UNPROFOR deployed in. Mr. Kirudja testified that Spiro Nikovic, as the commander of the 10th Corps, put those plans into practice according to the instructions from the Federal Secretariat of the National Defence from Belgrade. Mr. Kirudja also testified here that the JNA indeed withdrew from the territory of Krajina and Croatia, as planned by Mr. Kadijevic and Mr. Adzic, the two being the chief of the General Staff and the secretary for National Defence, and as agreed with Mr. Nambiar, who was commander of the forces to be deployed in Yugoslavia. Last but not least, Mr. Kirudja confirmed that the Serbs from Krajina voluntarily withdrew their heavy artillery and tanks as well as mortars and armoured vehicles. They put them in warehouses, and that was done under the auspices of the UN. They also -- he also confirmed that the Serbs from Krajina asked that these weapons be returned by UNPROFOR at the moment the Croatian aggression against the Krajina and the UN protected areas began. Since we are discussing the hypothesis of the joint criminal enterprise, according to which the plan encompassed Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, which was supposed to have been cleansed of Serbs and joined with the new -- cleansed of non-Serbs and joined with the Serb state, Mr. Kirudja as regards that testified that Mr. Babic, as well as Mr. Fikret Abdic, who was the then-leader of the Cazina Krajina, on the 23rd of October, 1993, signed a peace agreement. Mr. Kirudja also testified that Fikret Abdic, as the leader, the Muslim leader, of the Cazina region of the so-called Cazin pocket, was of the political view that Croats, Serbs, and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as autochthonous populations should live together and in peace. Mr. Kirudja confirmed that such a political position of Fikret Abdic as a Muslim leader was contrary to the position of Alija Izetbegovic, the Muslim president of the Bosnian Presidency. Mr. Kirudja confirmed that due to his radicalism, Alija Izetbegovic had sent the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was loyal to Alija Izetbegovic, against the Muslim enclave known as Cazina -- Cazin Krajina, and that this 5th Corps of the Bosnian army, commanded by General Drekovic defeated militarily the forces of Fikret Abdic. Mr. Kirudja confirmed another fact, namely that Fikret Abdic had asked for military assistance from Serbs in the Krajina, in whose interest it was to support a moderate Muslim leader such as Fikret Abdic, and they assisted him to the best of their abilities. In the end, ultimately, they were defeated militarily. Contrary to such evidence from Mr. Kirudja, we heard some explanations given by Mr. Galbraith which are completely illogical and which are completely rather opposed to these claims of Mr. Kirudja. Mr. Galbraith was an ambassador to Croatia, not to Yugoslavia, and unlike the high UNPROFOR official, such as Mr. Kirudja, he focused only on Croatia not on Krajina. By testifying, Mr. Kirudja showed that this thesis on joint criminal enterprise, which allegedly was carried out by Milosevic and Martic in Bosnia-Herzegovina, is a complete fiction and has nothing to do with reality. Mr. Kirudja also said in evidence another matter, namely that in Bosnia everybody was armed; that both Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, as residents of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were all armed; and that it was a vicious circle of bloody vendettas and counter vendettas. This is what Mr. Kirudja told us in his evidence; therefore, all stories proposed by the Prosecution on some alleged joint criminal enterprise are completely unfounded. Now that we have touched upon this thesis of joint criminal enterprise, which allegedly was in force from 1990 to 1995, because that was the period of time to which the Prosecution evidence pertained, thus Mr. Kirudja confirmed that Mr. Milosevic, as president of Serbia at the elections for the president of Serbian Krajina in late 1993/early 1994, supported Milan Martic as a candidate in those elections. That is to say that he provided political support to Milan Martic, and Mr. Kirudja explained what were the reasons for Mr. Milosevic doing that. He did that in a situation where Mr. Martic was facing Mr. Babic as another candidate, who, according to Mr. Kirudja, had majority in -- among the opposition and the parliament of Serbian Krajina and who initiated political initiatives aimed at falsely accusing UNPROFOR and expelling it from the territory of Serbian Krajina. Mr. Kirudja therefore confirmed that the essence of the political support of Mr. Milosevic to Mr. Martic in political elections was aimed at preserving the UNPROFOR mission in Yugoslavia. Both Mr. Kirudja and American President -- American Ambassador, Mr. Galbraith, confirmed that Mr. Martic, as president of the Serbian Krajina, concluded two international agreements aimed at seeking peaceful solution. Zagreb agreement on the 29th of March, 1994, immediately after he was elected president, which envisaged end to hostilities and separation of forces on the front line, Serbian and Croatian forces. There was supposed to be a one kilometre separation line among them for infantry weapons, ten kilometres for mortars and tanks, and 20 kilometres for artillery. This agreement, this international agreement, was signed when Mr. Martic was in the office of the president of Serbian Krajina. Mr. Kirudja also testified that Mr. Martic was president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina when the November agreement was signed as well, on the measures for development and economic trust as the second phase of the peace initiative in Krajina. The purpose of this was to establish an economic ties between the Serbian Krajina and Croatia, by opening highways, gas pipes, and other economic activities, oil pipelines as well. Mr. Kirudja, as the OTP witness, also testified pertaining to this joint criminal enterprise that it would have been wholly erroneous to claim that Mr. Milosevic rejected the Z-4 plan. This was just an attempt on the part of Mr. Milosevic to create some space for him for political manoeuvres which would have an impact on the leadership of Serbian Krajina so as to accept precisely what the Z-4 plan proposed, namely an autonomy within the borders of Croatia. Mr. Kirudja confirmed that Mr. Milosevic was opposed to any kind of national approach in creating state structure, that, unlike some other presidents of some other republics, he was not a nationalist. Mr. Kirudja, as an OTP witness, also confirmed that under Tudjman's rule, Croatia was declared to be a state of Croatian people, and the Serbs rightfully emphasised that they wouldn't fare well in such a state; that's what Mr. Kirudja testified. Unlike Croatia, Serbia under Mr. Milosevic's rule was a civic state. Since Your Honours asked me once why we invoked Mr. Milosevic so often, I told you on that occasion, Your Honours, that Mr. Milosevic was designated as a leader within that joint criminal enterprise and that Mr. Martic simply assisted him within that joint criminal enterprise. Mr. Kirudja, both in his examination-in-chief and cross-examination, testified otherwise, quite otherwise. And Mr. Kirudja dismantled the OTP thesis on the joint criminal enterprise; he stated directly that Milosevic supported Krajina within Croatia -- in Croatia. The purpose of the joint criminal enterprise is completely opposite, and this is why this thesis of the OTP does not stand. Mr. Kirudja, as an OTP witness, spoke of Vance Plan. Once again I'm reminding you that he was a highly educated official who testified about the UN peace mission in Yugoslavia which had just a single goal, namely to disarm all armed formations, to ensure the withdrawal of the JNA, to ensure that the Serb TO weaponry was stored in warehouses under the UNPROFOR double-key principle. So through all these means and through ensuring peaceful return of refugees, this mission was supposed to bring about a peaceful resolution to the Yugoslav crisis without prejudging its outcome. This is something quite opposite, radically different, from what is stated by the Prosecution and Mr. Maci Ratcliff [phoen]. Mr. Kirudja explained that the Security Council in its Resolution 762 from 1992, 26th of June, 1992, which condemned the Croatian aggression against the Miljevac plateau, which took place on the 21st of June, 1992, in addition to this resolution, the Security Council also adopted another decision on pink zones. Mr. Kirudja explained that this decision of the Security Council, namely the one on pink zones, was contrary to the Vance Plan, that is to say the UN peacekeeping mission in Yugoslavia. It was contrary in such a way that the Security Council decided in advance that the pink zones would be immediately placed back under the Croatian control. Unlike all other UNPA zones, the status of which was supposed to be resolved through an overall solution to the Yugoslav crisis through political negotiations, and also within the negotiations held at the conference for the former Yugoslavia. By explaining in such terms the UN decision on pink zones, Mr. Kirudja, as an OTP witness, said in evidence that such a decision by Security Council against local Serbs in Croatia was seen as a betrayal of Serbian interests and that, in those pink zones, it was used as a trigger, it served as a trigger for local population, which, in Mr. Kirudja's words, resorted to ensuring order through its own means, by -- and then all these other developments, such as arsons and other cases of disorder, were aimed at not allowing Croatia to take over control over those territories. Mr. Kirudja, through his evidence, said that this was no joint criminal enterprise, nothing of the sort; rather, this was a political reality or rather this was a political reaction of the population, a spontaneous one that had nothing to do with the authorities. This was confirmed by the report of Mr. Viktor Andreev, who was also a UN official. Mr. Kirudja confirmed another matter when it comes to joint criminal enterprise, namely that there was another function that the UN peacekeeping mission in Yugoslavia had, namely that in the territories where the UN forces were deployed - that is to say in the Krajina region - regardless of any differences in faith, gender, political orientation, and so on, the purpose of the UN mission was to chase away any political fears that may have existed not only among Croats or Serbs but among all people living in that area. Mr. Kirudja confirmed that while UNPROFOR was present in protected zones, there were five aggressions carried out by Croatian army against such zones. The first one was an aggression against the Miljevac plateau which was condemned by the UN Security Council Resolution 762, dated the 26th of June, 1992. On that occasion, Croatian forces killed and threw in a pit 40 Serbs. Another major aggression was in the Maslenica region, from Maslenica Zrelo [phoen] to Sinj, which is an area of about 100 kilometres. On the 21st of January, 1993, an aggression was carried out during which ten Serbian villages in Kotor area were torched to the ground, churches destroyed, population expelled, driven out, and there were 491 Serb victims as a result of that aggression. Nobody ever from the political highest echelons of Croatia was ever held responsible for that, nor will they be. And only under those circumstances, where such people are not held responsible, can the OTP put forward such a thesis. UNPROFOR confirmed that refugees from Ravni Kotar, which were Serbian refugees driven out of their homes -- driven out of their homes by Croatian aggression against Maslenica, so when such people, refugees, came to Knin and in a desperate state expelled Croats from their homes, the Prosecution accused Krajina Police for this, even though UN reports stated that they found such Croats in Vrpolje, they found an accommodation there in safe havens and that they were protected there by Serb policemen. Even though the Prosecution has in their possession the UN reports stating that the Serb authorities were powerless to stop this, which came as a result of Croatian aggression, but that they promised that they would ensure that everybody who was driven out of their homes would be enabled to return back, the Prosecution simply put everything upside down, absolutely everything. Mr. Kirudja confirmed that on 6 September 1993, and also on the 7th of September, several days before Croatia attacked the area known as Medak pocket, General Janko Bobetko, Chief of Staff of Croatian army, met with Mr. Kirudja. And then Mr. Kirudja, the witness, told us that that general with whom he had met earlier many times, the following words, namely he said this: "Tell the Serbs that the long Croatian arm will get them." I'm reminding you, Your Honours, that this was a Croatian general who held such views about Serbs, but who also had racist views about UNPROFOR units. He demanded from Mr. Kirudja and UNPROFOR mission to order all non-European forces to leave the territory of Croatia, all non-European UNPROFOR forces. So if the armed Kenyan UNPROFOR soldiers were threatened by this Croatian general, threatened as UN forces, then just imagine, Your Honours, what fate awaited local Serbs. You don't even have to consider this because Mr. Kirudja spelled it out for you. He said, as did the OTP witness McElligott, namely that they said that General Jean Cot, immediately after the Medak pocket operation, toured three Serbian villages, Citluk, Pocitelj, and Divoselo, and then he said that the destruction was systematic, complete, and deliberate. There was no trace of life, be it human or animal life in those settlements. This is the long Croatian arm chasing Serbs, Your Honours. This is what the OTP witness, Mr. Kirudja, testified about. Mr. Kirudja said against -- opposite of Mr. Milosevic many times; he testified about that. He said that he also knew how Mr. Milosevic acted during the Flash operation. He said that he knew that Mr. Milosevic was opposed to these military operations put in place by Croatia. Mr. Kirudja testified that there was also the fifths Croatian attack operation called Storm. Other OTP witnesses, namely expert Grujic, testified that in the Flash and Storm operations, between 250.000 and 300 [as interpreted] people were driven away from Krajina. When we have in mind the testimony of Mr. Veljko Dzakula, who was the first OTP witness, he stated that back in May 1993 the Security Council was shown data that the Croatian authorities in the Croatian towns and cities, outside the territory of Krajina, had expelled 251.000 Serbs, even if we do some simple math, that out of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the total number of Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- back in 1991. But by August 1995, the figure that was left can be arrived at by removing 250.000 expelled later on and 251.000 expelled by -- from 1995. Mr. Kirudja, as well as other OTP's witnesses, testified that the Tudjman's political project and the HDZ project, to create Croatia as the state of Croatian peoples with the Serbian portion of less than 7 per cent, was exactly being put in place, and this was indirectly proven by the OTP itself through their own witnesses. Mr. Kirudja testified as to yet another important thing. After the beginning of the crisis and UNPROFOR deployment in Yugoslavia, there was an embargo on the import of weapons in the affected territories in Slovenia and Croatia, but he confirmed that Croatia was heavily armed and that they were continuously purchasing new weapons. And we all were witnesses to the final outcome. Mr. Kirudja, as well as other OTP witnesses, have shown that the biggest problem of the UNPROFOR mission, once deployed in Krajina, was the presence of about 16.000 special police troops, for which Mr. McElligott said that, apart from the 7.000 regular police, the 16.000 carried automatic rifles but they did not go about conducting police work. They controlled the territory and they patrolled the area. Even Mr. McElligott, as an OTP witness, confirmed that there is an UNCIVPOL report from September 1991 in which the pressure on the Serbs in Krajina was increasing greatly, that there were daily incursions by Croatian forces, be it militarily or in terms of introducing groups of civilians in the territory. Both witnesses confirmed that the basic request of the civilian police of the UN was to disband the military police units. Mr. Kirudja testified that General Djukic in October 1992 conveyed a decision to him by Mr. Martic, who was the then-minister of the interior, to disband those units, because that was agreed with the UNPROFOR force commander in Yugoslavia. Mr. Kirudja also testified that such a decision by Milan Martic was met with astonishment and refusal by the local Serb commanders, but nonetheless, the decision was implemented, as evidenced by some written proof and confirmed by Mr. Kirudja. If you have in mind all these facts relating to the act and conduct of the accused, Martic, and other alleged perpetrators of the criminal enterprise and if we have in mind the political developments in Yugoslavia during that time - which is something you need to do, Your Honours, because the OTP hypothesis on the joint criminal enterprise deals with an alleged political plan elevated to the international level and arena with some horrific consequences - then the only conclusion you can arrive at, based on all the evidence presented here by the OTP, that it caved in, it ran completely contrary to the situation on the ground. The hypothesis of the joint criminal enterprise was brought down by the OTP witnesses themselves. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kirudja's very testimony shows that the hypothesis on the joint criminal enterprise, as presented here, is completely fictional. Other Prosecutor's witnesses show that further. Their military expert, Mr. Theunens, analysed all constitutional and legal regulation pertaining to the functioning of the armed forces in Yugoslavia, as well as the functioning of civilian and military authorities in Yugoslavia. Mr. Theunens established beyond dispute - and he mentioned that in his evidence when answering questions by the OTP and the Defence - that the JNA was a regular armed force of Yugoslavia and that back in 1990, 1991, and 1992, was deployed in the territory of its own state. He also stated that the Yugoslav armed forces were unified comprising the JNA and the TO, being the two components, and that both components were part of the Yugoslav federal armed forces. He also explained and confirmed what is stipulated in the Yugoslav constitution, and that is that the armed forces were commanded over by the Presidency which at wartime becomes the Supreme Command staff and including the Federal Secretariat. Furthermore, Mr. Theunens confirmed that republics, members to the Yugoslav federation, played no role in commanding the armed forces. Mr. Theunens, as an OTP expert, confirmed that after Croatia's independence was declared - or should I call it secession? - which was done unilaterally on the 25th of June, 1991, that Mr. Tudjman, as the HDZ and Croatian president, invited the Croatian population to mutiny, and that was stated by Mr. Theunens. He didn't declare himself on whether he thought it was a military mutiny because he thought it fell outside the scope of his investigation, but the next witness stated that it was a classical armed rebellion or mutiny. Another witness also confirmed that all the JNA troops and facilities in Croatia were blocked and put in danger, put under attack. Witness Theunens confirmed that there were 14 truces signed by the JNA who was the then absolutely superior armed force, compared to the illegal armed forces of Croatia at the time, that such truce was accepted by them. Witness Theunens also confirmed that this worked to the benefit of the Croatian side. Colonel Maksic, another OTP witness, stated that the JNA initiated the operation to deblock the blocked facilities in September 1991 and that it held such superiority that in very short time, with the use of its artillery and rocket system, could have destroyed completely the armed forces of the secessionist Croatia, but the military and political leadership of Yugoslavia would not allow that. In September or in early October, the JNA advancement towards Zadar was wrought to a halt, as testified by Witness Maksic. That took place at the moment when the Croatian paramilitary armed forces of the ZNG and the police were fleeing Zadar on boats, sailing towards the Adriatic islands. After that, we have the situation in Skabrnja. Mr. Theunens' entire evidence, being the military expert; as well as Colonel Maksic's evidence; as well as the testimony of another important OTP witness, Mr. Dzakula; as well as from the testimonies of many other ordinary people, witnesses here, some of whom were also victims, it is clear beyond dispute that the JNA was the armed -- legitimate armed force of the then-Yugoslavia acting in its capacity and within its territory at the time of Croatia's secession. The hypothesis on the joint criminal enterprise makes no sense with the view of such evidence of many of OTP's witnesses. In their indictment, they allege crimes in 19 counts. All those 19 counts are directly linked, according to them, with the joint criminal enterprise. They also state that the alleged facts in the 19 counts, that they comprise acts committed in order to realise or to implement such a joint criminal enterprise. In item 1 they mention expulsions; then they mention murders, persecutions; then between counts 5 and 9 they mention imprisonment, torture, inhumane acts, and cruel treatment; in counts 10 to 11 they mention deportation and forcible transfer; in counts 12 to 14, they speak of wanton destruction, plunder of public or private property; and to conclude, in counts 15 to 19, they mention unlawful attacks on civilians, murder, inhumane acts, and cruel treatment. What is most interesting is the hypothesis put forth by the OTP in its pre-trial brief and the indictment, and that is that all these individual acts were but pieces of puzzle -- of a puzzle, of the so-called joint criminal enterprise; and this also runs contrary to their hypothesis. They offered a footage of an intercepted meeting between Mr. Spegelj and Minister Boljkovac, both were then-ministers in Croatia, and that took place in October and November 1991. The OTP established that the footage is authentic and was put at their disposal by the FBI or the CIA; therefore, there was no meddling with it. It pertains to the October/November 1991 and was shown for the first time in January 1992. It was footage which shocked the Yugoslav as well as the European public, in my view. You have seen the transcript from the footage, and you've heard the witnesses confirm what took place there, including Mr. Dzakula. They stated that General Spegelj, who was the then-Croatian defence minister, stated that not a single JNA officer was to reach their barracks alive; that was in 1991 -- 1990. And he also states that they have assigned two persons for each officer who were to knock on his door and kill him and then move on to the next. That is the contents of the footage. The transcript and the witnesses confirmed it. It was also confirmed that Spegelj planned for a merciless show-down with the JNA. He literally states this is a civil war, there is no mercy for women and children. We should fire shells at apartments. And in November 1990, Mr. Boljkovac, the then-minister of the interior, replies: We will butcher Knin. It will never be what it used to be again. It also proves massive purchases of weapons by Croatia and the importation of those weapons from Hungary. These facts confirming the arming of the HDZ and various Croatian villages were confirmed by various

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Therefore, this was Witness MM-80, who spoke about the fact that as a JNA officer in March, April, and May of 1991, he was in the territory of Krajina, inside the barracks and the garrison in Knin; that as a JNA officer he was threatened by phone, solely because he was a Serb and a JNA officer. He also testified that a male voice spoke on the phone to his daughter and said that: We will butcher your parents, and then some screams were heard, after which the child suffered a shock and began stuttering, from which she took months to recover. This was Witness MM-80, who confirmed that this was the regular climate in Croatia at the time. Having in mind his position, he's a relevant witness because he has data confirming what he had seen; and in his responses in the questions put by the OTP and the Defence, he confirmed that the HDZ, as the leading party in Croatia, was illegally arming Croatian population. This was a party arming Croatian population with illegal weapons in various local communes and municipalities. There witness confirmed that in the village of Skabrnja there was an independent Skabrnja battalion numbering 250 people approximately , and his evidence is -- or rather, he heard this from a JNA officer who was a member of the service informed about that. A lot of other witnesses, Croats, also confirmed this, those who belonged to that unit; the commander of the Saborsko battalion did, as did Luka Brkic, a member of that unit. Now we are turning to the portion of the indictment which speaks of the events in a number of villages, Bruska, Skabrnja, Nadin, Saborsko, Poljanak, Lipovaca, Bacin, Dubica, Cerovljani. The general thesis of the Prosecution when it comes to events in these villages is within the thesis on joint criminal enterprise. This is the general description they provide. They say that the Serb forces, which belong within the JNA - I don't know how this is possible, but according to the Prosecution it is possible - but namely they claim that the Serb forces put under siege undefended villages; start firing; and then when the population flees, they enter villages and start torching everything. But through their witnesses they painted a completely different picture. Not only did Martin Spegelj, a minister of defence, and Minister Boljkovac, minister of the interior of Croatia, through their conversation prove that Croatia started arming itself back in 1990, seven to eight months before they decided to secede. So it's not only them who testify about this, but it's also the residents of Skabrnja itself who spoke directly of this. Commander of the independent battalion in Skabrnja, Mr. Marko Miljanic, said that he had under his command about 800 people, that the Skabrnja battalion was assigned a territory of seven villages, that these seven villages represented one-third of the Zadar municipality, that these villages included Skabrnja, Nadin, Galovica, Gorica, Zemunik Donji, Prkos, a total of 800 people. A member of the Independent Skabrnja Battalion who testified in these proceedings, Luka Brkic, said that members of that battalion had uniforms from eastern Germany with the eastern German helmets, boots, belts, and automatic rifles. As this was taking place in Skabrnja, east Germany no longer existed for quite a long time. It was part of unified Germany, and at the time it was the major force in the break-up of Yugoslavia. Germany was the first country to recognise the independence of Croatia on the 15th of January, 1992. And a little bit prior to that, they provided uniforms and weapons to the rebel forces in Croatia. Was that purely accidental? Mr. Brkic, as an OTP would be, also confirmed how the armed formations in Skabrnja went into combat. They went -- automatic rifles. Based on the diary of Lieutenant-Colonel Vukovic, we know that they had in addition to automatic rifles, also mortars, that 37 hand grenades were seized, and also a recoilless gun as well as a number of other weaponry and ammunition. According to another member of the Skabrnja Battalion, 14 to 15 defenders died in that operation. In order to understand the situation, in order to see this in reality, just picture yourself a village in Texas where 14, 15 defenders in a village die in fighting with federal forces. So that is the situation that existed in the -- in Yugoslavia in 1991, the identical one. What we know about members of the Skabrnja Battalion is that they had uniforms on them. This is what they wore. And when they clashed with the JNA, when it seemed as though they would be defeated, then these members started taking off uniforms on the spot. Some of them would still wear some pieces of a uniform, and they would enter basements where civilian population were hiding. So in a basement where Luka Brkic was, an armed member of the Skabrnja Battalion, the JNA found two automatic rifles and a machine-gun. This constitutes a direct threat to their own civilian population. And in that situation, where a member of a warring faction comes to testify here as one of the main Prosecution witnesses, naturally such a witness will always be biased whenever necessary. However, such witnesses portrayed to you the essence of what was taking place in Skabrnja. Based on the notes of Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic, these notes were admitted into evidence here; and based on them, we know that the operation of cleansing of Skabrnja and Nadin - Nadin was not a village with hunting rifles, which is what a witness from Zagreb told us, testifying through videolink, this was not a village with just five to six rifles, no. This was a place where according to Witness MM-80, there were many attacks against the road leading to Zadar and Zadar airport. This witness said that the fiercest operations were so strong that they discontinued any traffic on that road, and those operations were launched from Skabrnja and Nadin. This witness also confirmed that this operation was aimed at cleansing out Croatian armed forces which, according to Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic, were Ustashas; this is how he called them. Witness MM-80 also testified about these roads leading to Zadar. He said that they were not only disrupted and threatened, but that the JNA with its vehicles and in columns had to travel through fruit orchards and fields. Witness Marko Miljanic, commander of the Skabrnja Battalion, testified about how he set or, rather, placed two minefields, including one behind Zemunik. Witness MM-80, the man who as an officer had such information available to him, the man whose child was threatened - you know who I have in mind - this witness testified upon seeing a document of General Vukovic that four days before the 20th November, 1991 - and you know that the operation in Skabrnja was on the 18th and 19th, so this means from the 16th of November, 1991, onwards - they attacked incessantly the JNA airport in Zemunik, in the background of which Skabrnja Battalion was deployed with minefields. They damaged very valuable military equipment. They put at risk the lives of people, animals, officers, and property. Witness MM-80 confirmed a fact from that report, namely that in Zadar 14 JNA barracks were blocked. This was the purpose for which units in Skabrnja, in Nadin, and Kijevo were used, Your Honours. Once again, a protected witness, MM-78, told us that an alleged police station in Kijevo disrupted JNA communication with Drnis. This spoke of a normal, civilised altitude that the JNA had toward the civilian population. Now that we are dealing with Skabrnja and Nadin, this has to do with the counts of indictment which also cover Bruska and Bacin, but these are no military operations. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC

And then the Prosecution asked them whether somebody was charged with this, and that's an irrelevant question because the investigative judge only has to investigate what happened on the spot. And then it's up to the Prosecution and the Court to see whether any charges need to be brought and how they are going to act in relation to these charges. I forgot to mention something when it comes to this event in Bruska. We saw a lot of documents; a lot of documents were introduced through Witness MM-80. This witness confirmed that this case was investigated, that there were a lot of suspects, and that the names of possible perpetrators are well-known. What's more, however, to claim that somebody didn't want to resolve this is ridiculous, for a simple fact, because Marinovici, the victims who appeared here, Ante, Jasna Marinovic, and other people who testified here all said that they had been providing information to Croatian authorities. If the Serbian authorities failed to find perpetrators because, as the Prosecutor claimed, they were protected by Serbs, then Croatian authorities would have found them if this were so simple. I have to urge you to bear in mind that this was a war situation, that these were very difficult times and a completely irregular circumstances in which the civilian population and everybody else lived. Your Honours, I don't know if this is a convenient time for our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my address so far, Your Honours, I covered the first three locations, Skabrnja, Bruska, Nadin; and when it comes to events in Bruska, we were able to see that this was a horrific crime, a horrific crime. We were also able to see that this horrific crime was investigated by the investigative authorities of Serbian Krajina. There was an investigative judge and a criminal technician and so on. In addition to them, military authorities also investigated this. The victims, in addition to providing information to them, also provided information to Croatian authorities investigating this crime in Zadar, and there have been no results. Perhaps it may sound cynical when we say that they did not wish to resolve this. I told you earlier that the job of police is to conduct an investigation and it needs to be done in accordance with the laws in force. They need to carry out an investigation on the site and they need to try and find perpetrators, but the circumstances at the time were highly irregular, abnormal. I have to remind you of something. Several decades ago, president of the United States was killed; also several decades ago, Aldo Moro, president of Italy, was killed; as was Olof Palme, Prime Minister of Sweden and their murderers have not been found to this day, even though this was a highly investigated -- all of these events were highly investigated. It is not always possible to find the perpetrators. Another event that the Prosecution claims is linked to the joint criminal enterprise are in Saborsko and Poljaca and Poljanac. The witnesses confirmed that in Saborsko, which is a Croatian village, in terms of its residents, there was a police station which then, in April 1992, was established. In addition to them, there was also a unit called Saborsko company. This Saborsko company received reinforcement numbering 120 to 150 armed people from Zagreb. They arrived in a convoy consisting of several trucks carrying weapons, ammunition, people. And then they received assistance on another occasion. In Saborsko, there was a special unit of Croatian MUP from Duga Resa. Following this, another special unit arrived to assist them. Based on the war diary of tactical group 2 of the JNA under the command of Cedomir Bulat, it was established that several days before the operation against Saborsko began, very fierce fire was opened, launched from Saborsko, against the JNA barracks. The combat that ensued was a fierce one. That means that in Saborsko, as well as in Skabrnja, we had irregular armed Croatian troops consisting of the HDZ and ZNG members. They turned a peaceful village into military barracks and military facility. The witnesses from Saborsko told us about Tuk, about Alan, about Brdine, and neighbouring settlements around Saborsko. There were seven to eight positions with mortars, anti-aircraft machine-guns, machine-gun nests, and so on. We heard that there was a very severe clash, following which Croatian forces in that village were defeated. We also heard from witnesses that Saborsko, as well as Poljanak and Lipovaca, had its own units, that is to say that in Poljanak and Lipovaca there were also local units. We heard this from local residents who said that they were members of the village guard. When, in a state, forces are formed against that state, then things become quite serious. It ceases to be a minor thing, and those who undertake such action should bear full responsibility for that conduct. The operations that is were conducted in Saborsko, Lipovaca, Poljanak, and other places certainly cannot be an excuse for any crimes committed, but all of the witnesses heard here said that these were acts taken by irresponsible individuals who were beyond anybody's control. It was difficult to establish who these people were. In Skabrnja, in Nadin, in Saborsko, in Poljanak, there were armed formations of Croatian government, which were outside of control of the federal government, and they acted against federal armed forces. Once an armed conflict erupted, then naturally there had to be victims and it's not something that I approve, no. This is not something that I condone. It is just a fact that civilians always perish in armed conflicts wherever they may take place throughout the world. The Prosecutor once again tried to portray the situation as a situation in which peaceful Croatian villages were attacked by this criminal army, who -- which wanted to cleanse the entire territory from Croatian population. The next location mentioned by the OTP in the indictment, in a separate count and in separate locations in which civilians were killed according to the joint criminal enterprise recipe, are Dubica and Cerovljani. Concerning such plight of civilians, which are beyond dispute, as well as that those in Saborsko in terms of horrific suffering of civilians, as well as in Bacin, Dubica, and Cerovljani, the situation was repeated. Witness Josip Josipovic confirmed that the HDZ, led by the Crisis Staff which was in Hrvatska Kostajnica, and the staff being headed by Mr. Koljevica [as interpreted], was arming population in all three locations. They were arming the local Croatian population by the leading Croatian party the HDZ, which was then in power. In 1991, all this was taking place within the territory of a sovereign European state called Yugoslavia. Witness Josipovic, as well as MM-025, confirmed that the civilian population was armed by the HDZ and that the civilian population from Bacin, Dubica, and Cerovljani, on orders of Croatian authorities were evacuated on the 14th of September, 1991. The crime in Bacin took place as late as the 20th of October, 1991. There were no -- there was no military activity, and there was no logic or purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then counts 15 to 19, these are linked directly with the joint criminal enterprise, and they concern themselves with the attack on Zagreb. In paragraph 50 of the indictment, the Prosecutor stated that on the 1st of May, 1995, the Croatian army launched an attack against the SVK in Western Slavonia. In paragraphs 51, 52, 53, and 54, the Prosecutor describes the attack on Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May. In that part of the indictment, they claim that there was no military necessity for the attacks, that they were illegal, and that their aim was retaliation. In order to see the position of the Defence in a proper -- in the proper way, we wanted to comment these paragraphs as well as the evidence concerning these paragraphs. At that moment, Croatia was already an internationally recognised state. At that moment, in the territory of Croatia, there were UNPROFOR troops. At that moment, it's been four years without any attack, military attack, on Zagreb. At that moment, we have the Zagreb agreement in place concerning the separation of the warring parties, which was implemented only by the Serbian side. At that time, the economic agreement was also put in place between the Croats and the Serbs; and as witnessed by Mr. Kirudja as well as Mr. Galbraith, it was the time of political negotiations to resolve the crisis. Therefore, without any real justification, apart from a very distinct wish to complete his plan from 1991 and 1992, that is to have the independent Croatia without the Serbs, the Tudjman group, the Tudjman -- Tudjman and people around him launch an operation object the 1st of May. Mr. Grujic confirmed that he saw 168 excavated corpses, and 11 years later their names are still not known. The autopsies have not been carried out in 11 years. Witness Poje, who was an OTP expert, explained that the artillery attack on Zagreb represented general artillery support to support the Serbian Krajina units which were deployed in Western Slavonia. You saw the footage, you read the transcript, and you heard Mr. Martic's speech on the radio in which he explained that because of Tudjman -- the way Tudjman behaved in Western Slavonia and because he attacked civilian population there, they had to resort to launching attacks against settlements in Croatia in order to bring the Croatian aggression to a halt, and indeed it did. He also said that should it continue, the Republic of Serbian Krajina will be forced to continue with their attacks. We saw that several times during the OTP case. Although on several occasions in our cross-examination we were not allowed to put questions to establish the link between the two events, the cause and effect principle was not allowed. At that moment, the OTP case was still ongoing and our case was not known. Therefore, this position of the Chamber raised doubts as to an attitude or a view taken by the Chamber in this case. Nevertheless, we had full faith in your judgement. And we have your instructions in mind, and we were told that the fact that the people responsible for Western Slavonia were not invited is something that falls within the scope of the OTP, when nevertheless they will never have to face justice. We saw documents mentioning 11 and a half thousand people who were expelled from Okucani; they were Serbs. After the Flash operation, only 800 remained. Those are UN civilian police data in -- from June and July 1995. You saw a Defence document from the 4th of May, 1995; this is Defence Exhibit 112 dated the 5th of May, mentioning an event of the 4th of May, in which there were eye-witnesses of Croatian artillery attacks against Serb villages instead of Serb military facilities. Generals Al Rodan and Denaro, as well as General Natalon and other Argentinian members of the UNPROFOR Battalion were witnesses to this. You were also presented with evidence that the Croatian forces used water to wash Serb blood from various villages. At the same time, another hundred corpses were found, including women and children. In the village of Trnovace, 50 civilians were massacred. The Serb forces of Krajina could do nothing else but to try and launch attacks against such targets that they could with the weapons they had at their disposal. Mr. Poje, as an artillery expert, showed that the rocket system used to attack Zagreb has only two types of rockets, one which is a cluster one used to launch anti-tank mines, and a cluster charge, which was the only one that could have been used, which is used to pierce armour. Another witness of the OTP, Mr. Branko Lazarevic, a policeman, showed us on the map that in the centre of town there was the Ministry of Defence, which is 400 by 300 metres in the very heart of town at the end of the Ilica; and then the Ministry of the Interior, the size of 150 by 40 metres is also in the centre of town; that there are Banski Dvori in the centre of town where the Croatian government sits. The city MUP was also affected by the attack. The military airport of Pleso was also hit; it has both civilian and military purpose. They also managed to hit the business area where INA, the oil company's reservoirs were located. This was a forced move, and still we have the fact that the OTP never indicted anyone from these horrific crimes in Western Slavonia. This also serves to indicate that the indictment will never be raised, otherwise they would have to withdraw the indictment against Mr. Babic because -- Mr. Martic because they haven't chosen to persecute those who prompted Mr. Martic to such actions as occurred at a later stage when Zagreb was attacked. Another thing is very interested as to their hypothesis on the joint criminal enterprise and the various counts of the indictment, and that is when we talk about the method they use or they chose to apply. They seem to try and use the perpetuum mobile principle. They don't want to specify who, when, how, where, with whom, and in which way created this plan on the joint criminal enterprise. The only thing they do is they claim that it exists and that Martic and Milosevic, inter alia, tried to see it through. Then in the continuation of the indictment, they stipulate the locations we've mentioned, where there were individual deaths of civilians and soldiers, and they call that the crime base. Then they apply a technique in which they don't really want to discover the true perpetrators of the crimes, even though they have a full list of potential suspects. It is quite clear why they don't want that: Because, by determining the true perpetrator, they should -- they would have to establish the causal link and there goes their joint criminal enterprise story. In such a situation, we only have the civilian victims identified, and on the basis of that, the OTP tries to prove that this was the result of the joint criminal enterprise. First they do nothing to prove the existence of the enterprise, and then they mention a list of victims to prove the first one. That is why I said they used this never-ending principle of perpetuum mobile without any loss of energy. As the potential perpetrators of everything stipulated in the indictment, in particular in paragraph 16 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- they state that the Serb police forces of the Krajina, which, as the OTP says, were called the Martic's men, or SAO Krajina Militia, and from -- and thenceforth they use the common term "Martic's Police"; such an identification of perpetrator is not allowed in such a proceeding as this. Any unit, any formation, has a name and it has to be identified. Not a single document of the Prosecution pertaining to the Secretariat of the Interior of SAO Krajina, Ministry of the Interior of SAO Krajina, not a single document - and Ari Kerkkanen looked through all of them, as did Mr. Theunens - none of these documents mentioned Martic's Police. This is a term coined by the Prosecution, used by them in order to portray certain police forces as a private police force under the command by the accused, Milan Martic, who established them and used them. The fact that it is so is further confirmed by paragraphs 11 and 13 of the indictment, where the Prosecutor specifically states that the decisions of competent organs such as Executive Council or the Assembly of SAO Krajina or the government, cabinet of SAO Krajina, appointed Milan Martic as minister of defence, be it of SAO Krajina or Serbian Krajina. The Prosecutor, through witnesses, Kerkkanen and Theunens, showed that there was a law on ministries within Serbian Krajina, that there was a law on internal affairs, and that those employed in the Ministry of the Interior were full-time employees of that entity. These people are policemen by profession, with full-time employment. So this is a professional organisation, numbering also reserve policemen, but they are not Martic's Police, no. They are policemen of the Ministry of the Interior. Witness McElligott spoke of 7.000 professional policemen, people who mostly worked for police stations in the former Yugoslavia. They were trained and did their job properly. We saw here documents through which witnesses of the Prosecution confirmed that the Ministry of the Interior of Serbian Krajina, under Martic as minister, sent policemen for further training in higher police schools in Banja Luka, in Belgrade, and so on. So these are people who are police professionals and to call them Martic's Police is to resort to personal terms. These are -- this is street terminology. Witness MM-046, when asked by Defence in cross-examination, as to who these Martic's men were - now this is a witness who has a college diploma - so when asked this he said that this was a street term, a colloquialism they used in Serbian Krajina. And the next witness, Krstic, Stanko, testified about being arrested by the paramilitary. When asked who was the paramilitary, he said: Local Serbs. And then when asked: Was it police or paramilitary? He said that he didn't distinguish, that it was all the same to him; and then he added that those were local shepherds wearing uniforms. So Martic's Police, as a common term for participants in joint criminal enterprise, is actually a street term, colloquialism, used in the former Yugoslavia by certain warring factions to denote the opposing force. In this instance, in this conflict, Croatia was one of the warring factions, and they used this term, Martic's Police, to denote an opposing force. This term cannot be used to denote a force that was established under legal laws and constitution. And in other portions of the indictment which speaks of the responsibility of Mr. Martic, I think that's paragraph 3. The Prosecutor says there that Mr. Martic was a minister of the interior or secretary of the interior in the so-called Serbian Krajina, and also president of the republic. So when they have to define what SAO Krajina was, the Prosecutor calls it "so-called SAO Krajina," which means that they deny its existence. So how can something that is so-called entitles Martic to de jure authorities? How are we going to resolve this issue? There is a simple explanation why the Prosecutor does not want to state that SAO Krajina existed. It had its government, cabinet; it had its Assembly; it had its laws and constitution. It had all legal authorities and all of this existed, but it doesn't suit the Prosecution because then we come to an issue that will challenge the joint criminal enterprise thesis: How is it possible that Croatia was recognised as an independent state in January of 1992 when it did not control one-third of its territory? And who recognised Croatia within the international community, despite the suggestion of the UN Secretary-General? Precisely because the UN peacekeeping mission was deployed there. This opened Pandora's box, and the Prosecutor is fully aware of this. This is why they term SAO Krajina as a so-called and they claim that Martic had de facto powers. Now, this method that is used in order to phrase the indictment was replicated in the use of witnesses. The Defence will show you that our submissions now are not closing arguments. The joint criminal enterprise has to be analysed through the prism of methodology used in writing this indictment. Now, after seeing all this evidence, the question becomes even more pertinent. The Prosecutor used many protected witnesses, among them Witness MM-003, concerning whom another protected witness, MM-078, said that he was violent-prone, a violent-prone person, also prone to abuse and theft. Witness MM-003 tried to get legal residence in a foreign country, that was denied, and then he said: "I had an agreement with the Prosecution. They were to ensure that I get legal residence in a foreign country, and I will testify about what they want me to do." This is plain improper conduct, Your Honours. They are trading here in order to obtain testimony that suits them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: (redacted), and three times during his evidence he asked that the Prosecution act in accordance with their promises, namely to assist him in resolving his status. So this similarity is shocking. Previous witness, MM-003, claimed that he had fled Yugoslavia with a falsified passport; that he provided incorrect information to immigration authorities; that he provided incorrect information to the OTP in order to become a witness; and in return for that, they were to help him solve his status. This is the method that the Prosecution uses in order to prove their joint criminal enterprise thesis. I'm not going to mention this witness's position because that would reveal his identity. Mr. Babic was a key witness of the Prosecution based on Parker's commission. We were able to see that he resided in a private home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, again out of an abundance of caution if we could redact page 42, line 20. I think it describes the -- well, I won't -- it describes the position of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May line 20 of page 42 please be deleted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we can perhaps start from 19, according to Judge Hoepfel. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next Prosecution witness, the key, their main insider, Mr. Milan Babic, according to the Parker commission report was in a private home from 1st December 1993 until July of 2004, when he reached a plea agreement with the Prosecution and had his trial. In January 2003 he signed a plea agreement with the Prosecution. Already in march, Parker's commission established that he complained of psychiatric problems. In September of 2004, he already threatened to commit suicide; his Defence council informed Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff of this. This witness, who is not emotionally balanced, was a protected witness in other trials, despite his health status, and came here as the main witness in Martic's trial. Parker's commission stated that he believed himself to be endangered. He believed that the Prosecution used him. His family members said that it was precisely during his testimony that the status of his family was solved, namely whether they were going to get a visa for living in a third country. This situation was a huge burden, both for the family of Mr. Babic and Mr. Babic himself. The conclusion of Parker's commission that there were no signals that he would commit a suicide is a surprising one, to say the least, but this is not the gist of what I'm saying. The gist of what I'm saying is: How is it possible that a person who is emotionally unbalanced, obviously, is brought here to testify in this case before this Tribunal? And to end his life in the middle of cross-examination by putting a nylon bag over his head and suffocating himself with a belt? This is the kind of a witness that they brought here. Another witness, a protected witness of the Prosecution, I hesitate to mention anything else in order not to reveal his identity, Witness MM-078 said about him that he was an extremely ambitious man. Mr. Kirudja said that Mr. Babic was the only politician in Krajina who opposed the UN initiative for peace, and he was the only politician who wanted to chase away UNPROFOR from Krajina in 1994. This is a man who is emotionally unbalanced, an unfortunate man who ended his life in the way he did and he -- his evidence was completely contrary to the evidence of Mr. Kirudja. Mr. Kirudja and some other witnesses spoke of Mr. Lazarevic, who was planned to come to testify but did not come here. He testified in many other trials. Mr. Kirudja says that he looked like the Great Gatsby, a man who tried -- who portrayed himself falsely as an interpreter and interpreted at various meetings, who falsely portrayed himself as a friend of Mr. Bulat; according to Mr. Kirudja this man was a mercenary. Colonel Raseta said that this man was introduced to him as a lieutenant-colonel and as an official of the State Security Service, although he was never on the list. This witness, until the last day, remained on the list of witnesses as one of the most important witnesses that they were going to call; we put in a lot of effort to prepare for this witness. And let me point out one more thing to just show you the kind of methodology that the Prosecution uses to prove their indictment. Mr. Theunens came here to testify as a military expert; he is a full-time employee of the OTP. He's their investigator. Together with the OTP, he wrote the indictment against Mr. Martic and then came here to support it through his testimony. This is the kind of a witness that the OTP called here to testify. He's an employee of the OTP. When we cross-examined him, we asked him whether -- or rather, while we cross-examined him, he asked whether he could contact his colleagues in the OTP in order to prepare for the testimony of the next witness. Your Honours, this all speaks of the methodology that was used in order to draft this indictment and the methodology that was used for the Prosecution case. The Prosecution has no case, and if they were to look at things realistically they would apologise to Mr. Martic and set him free. And instead of that, we got here something quite different, namely the proposal of the OTP as to how Defence case should look, what our timetable should be. The Prosecutor set forth, in advance, exactly how much time we need for witnesses, for the conference, for our opening arguments, and so on. Unfortunately, the Trial Chamber went along with this, and this is how the Prosecution works. Based on everything said so far, the Defence moves the Trial Chamber to do the following: Given that the Prosecution, through their evidence, showed that there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction of Mr. Martic, the Defence hereby proposes that all charges against Mr. Martic be dropped. The Prosecution has to prove Mr. Martic's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt in this stage of proceedings. This stage of proceedings has terminated based on what we have seen so far. Instead of proving the guilt of Mr. Martic, it is up to the Defence to show that Mr. Martic is not guilty, that he is in fact innocent. And you will agree, Your Honours, that this is completely upside down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm going to start with making a few general observations. I'll then respond to some -- some but not all of the things that Defence counsel has raised. I'll then -- consistent with the standard under 98 bis, I will go through, as briefly as I can, Your Honours, the evidence that we believe supports the charges in the indictment. My first general observation -- just in case Defence counsel is holding his breath, the Prosecution will not apologise to Mr. Martic and will not assent to his release. It's not in our power to release him at this stage, but we will certainly not assent to it. My second observation is that I think that, with respect, with all due respect, Defence counsel has completely misunderstood what we are doing here today and what the 98 bis standard is; that was evident from the beginning and throughout the presentation. It became absolutely clear at the end of the presentation, when he suggested that the Prosecution has to prove Mr. Martic's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt at this stage of the proceedings. That is not the standard. And I'm well aware that the Chamber is no doubt aware what the proper standard is, but if I could just very briefly touch on what we believe the proper standard is. We believe the proper standard has been set down by the an Appeals Chamber in Celebici and Jelisic, in those two appeals, and the test to be applied, and this is citing, maybe even quoting directly, is: "Whether there is evidence, if accepted, upon which a reasonable Tribunal of fact could be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused on the particular charge in question." That is the standard that is set down by both Celebici and Jelisic. I would also direct the Trial Chamber to the Trial Chamber decision in Strugar - its date is 21st of June, 2004 - which goes through in quite some detail what the standard is. And what is clear is that the test at this stage is whether there is some evidence to support the charges, and when that evidence -- when the Prosecution's evidence is taken at its highest, that is if it is accepted. The Strugar Trial Chamber, in its decision, makes it clear that it is not the task of the Trial Chamber at this stage, it is premature -- it is not the task of the Trial Chamber at this stage to try to weigh out all of the evidence, to try to make judgements about credibility, to try to balance out -- resolve conflicts in the evidence. That is just not the -- that is just not the test and that's not what we are doing here. The -- as long as there is some evidence to support each count, that we submit is sufficient, unless - and this is discussed in the Strugar decision - unless the evidence is so inherently incredible that no -- that the Trial Chamber found that no reasonable Trial Chamber could ever rely on that. And that, the Strugar Trial Chamber makes clear, is a very rare situation, and, we would submit, does not apply to any of the evidence in this case. There is no evidence in this case which is so incredible that we rely on to support the counts that the Trial Chamber could find -- would find or could find that it cannot be relied upon. The third observation that I would make is that Defence counsel, perhaps because of a misunderstanding of what we are doing here today, spends a lot of time talking about crimes that he says occurred on the other side, that were committed by Croats. That is not something I will respond to, unless instructed by the Trial Chamber to do so. Because it's our position that certainly at this stage, that kind of evidence is irrelevant, and, most likely, even at the final stage all of that evidence will be irrelevant. Before I go on and make specific responses to a few of the points raised by Defence counsel I do want to say this: We do -- we have reviewed the evidence, and we have come to the conclusion that the -- we believe that the -- that there is evidence under the proper 98 bis standard which supports all of the counts in the indictment. There is no need, no basis, to dismiss any of the counts in the indictment. Having said that, there are two allegations, two specific allegations, contained in the indictment which we do not believe are supported by the evidence, and this is principally because a witness did not come and testify. And that is paragraph 39, subsections (d) and (e), the detention at Bosanska Kostajnica and Bosanski Novi police station; (f) we have previously abandoned even before the trial began. Those two allegations, which we had preserved during trial, we do not believe have been sufficiently established at -- even under the 98 bis standard. We will not continue on those two charges -- those two allegations. I had informed Defence counsel about this earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's get your position quite clear. You would support an acquittal on those two?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it -- I don't think that's the -- I don't think that's sort of the proper result because the -- it's not an acquittal on those two because that is part of a larger count. That goes to several counts, and there are -- there is other bases for supporting those counts. And if I may, because that's been raised by the Trial Chamber - and this is something perhaps I should have addressed with respect to the Rule 98 bis standard. In -- the Rule 98 bis previously spoke about charges which were not supported by the evidence. And there was some question about what that meant, whether that meant allegations, specific allegations, or whether that meant counts. In December 2004, the rule was amended, and the principal amendment was to change this process from a written process to an oral process. However, it did also change the word "charges" to "counts," and it's our position that the -- as long as the Trial Chamber is satisfied that there is evidence that -- under the standard that there is some evidence to support a conviction on the count, it does not need to examine in detail every single allegation, every single victim, every single name. It does not need to go into that kind of detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm trying to get your position with respect to paragraph 39(d) and (e). Is it the Prosecution's position that the factual allegations made in 39(d) and (e) have not been supported by evidence, and therefore the Chamber can take that those allegations have been -- have not been proved?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will also -- although we have taken the position with respect to counts, I will address in some detail specific crime bases and specific allegations because I think it will be of assistance to the Trial Chamber and to the Defence. I will not take the position, for example, that you could find sufficient basis of -- for murders in one crime base and that would be sufficient. We are going to address all of the crime bases, and we believe that there is sufficient evidence with respect to all the crime bases. I will say that in our view the Defence has raised what I would describe, and respectfully describe, as a somewhat scattershot approach to the indictment, raising various points, some of which we think are completely inappropriate at this stage, most of which, frankly. If -- I would -- as I've said, our view is that all the counts have been supported. If the Trial Chamber has -- what we would ask that if the Trial Chamber has any reservations about any specific count, that we be given an opportunity to respond to that. We will respond to all the Defence allegations, we will make our own points; however, there is a lot to cover here and I don't want to miss anything. And so if there -- I would ask if there is some specific concern with respect to any count, from the Trial Chamber, that I do not address, that we be given an opportunity to -- out of fairness to respond to that, because as I've said, our review -- the result of our review is that we have satisfied the standard with respect to all the counts in the indictment. Let me briefly respond to some of the points raised by the Defence.
