The first is that the Defence -- the Defence allege that the Prosecution did not state whether there was an oral or written plan supporting the joint criminal enterprise; this misstates the law. As I will discuss later, the -- under the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, a plan is not required, and I refer the Trial Chamber to the Stakic appeal judgement. All that is required is a common purpose, individuals acting with a common purpose, but no plan is required and certainly no oral or written plan. The Defence allege that it was absurd that Martic is being charged or indicted for commanding over JNA forces. He is not being charged with that; he's being charged with being a member of a joint criminal enterprise with JNA forces that committed crimes during the period charged in the indictment. The Defence raised a number of points which seem to be, frankly in defence of -- more in defence of Mr. Milosevic than of Mr. Martic, but they suggested that the joint criminal enterprise allegation was undermined by the fact that Mr. Milosevic, they say, supported the Z-4 plan in 1994 and 1995. However, they are ignoring the evidence of Mr. -- of Ambassador Galbraith, who explained - and this is at 3752 and 3753 - explained why Slobodan Milosevic took a different position later on with respect to the Krajina in 1994 and 1995 than he had in 1990, 1991. And this had to do with the fact that by then Croatia was a recognised country and his hopes of breaking off the Krajina had disappeared, and so his position therefore changed. The Defence also suggested that the signing of the Vance Plan in -- on the 23rd of November, 1991, somehow showed that Mr. Milosevic or other members of the joint criminal enterprise were really striving for peace, and that this somehow undermines the allegation of the joint criminal enterprise. In our view, the opposite is true. The -- what is striking about the Vance Plan and the fact that it's reached on the 23rd of November, 1991, is that it is negotiated not by Serb representatives from the Krajina, but that it's negotiated by Mr. Milosevic and it's signed by Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Kadijevic and Mr. Tudjman, on the other side, showing who is in control. It shows the influence and power of Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Kadijevic at that time in November of 1991. They are the ones calling the shots, and then they -- the evidence shows that they then persuade Mr. Martic to support the Vance Plan and that they then pushed through the Vance Plan. It is also false to say, in our submission, that Mr. Babic was opposed to the Vance Plan; the truth is more subtle. And in any event, the issue here is not so resolve that; it's whether there is evidence about it. There is evidence that Mr. Babic didn't oppose it. What he wanted was a different version of the Vance Plan. He had a different idea. He opposed it in its form, as it was presented to him, and -- but he had a different view of how it should be -- what the Vance Plan should look like. The Vance Plan of course -- there is evidence on the record that the Vance Plan was not in fact respected by this accused, Milan Martic, that it was not in force, that the goal of demilitarisation that was enshrined in the Vance Plan was not respected, that the forces in the SAO Krajina continued to carry long-barrel weapons, and that the JNA left behind weapons and personnel, and that the -- and that the equipment was simply painted blue to disguise the fact that it had actually been JNA equipment. The Vance Plan of course also allowed the Serbs to hang on to the military gains that they had won during -- during 1991, and -- during the conflict in 1991, and so for that reason, was something that of course was supported. In addition, the goal of allowing refugees to come back into the SAO Krajina was also not supported by Mr. Martic, and that evidence has been provided by Mr. Babic but also by Mr. Dzakula. There is evidence about that. It also should be clear that the Vance Plan, while the Vance Plan was in existence, the -- in 1992, in the spring of 1992, the corridor operation, the Posavina corridor operation, was undertaken in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is evidence on the record that Mr. Martic personally participated in that operation with forces under his command and that the purpose of that operation - and I would refer to the 2211 of the transcript - was precisely the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise, just to join up Serb lands, to join up the SAO Krajina with Serbia, to make -- to connect the corridor, to make a greater Serbia. So the notion that the -- adopting the Vance Plan somehow shows that there wasn't a joint criminal enterprise, that there wasn't this purpose, is not -- is not supported by the record. The Defence suggested at one point - and I believe that they were talking about -- specifically about Bosnia and Herzegovina, but perhaps suggesting that the same is true in Croatia - that there were bloody circles of vendettas and counter-vendettas, that everybody was committing crimes, and it was going back and forth in circles of history. I would suggest that this approach and this defence is utterly cynical, and it's not -- it's contradicted on the record by several witnesses who say, who have told this Trial Chamber that war was not inevitable, that conflict could have been avoided, that there was -- there were alternatives to extremism. I would refer to witness Dzakula at 391, Witness MM-078 at 4424, and Witness MM-003 at 1981. Even if that -- even putting aside the evidence from those witnesses, I suggest that it's -- again that it's cynical to say that everybody was extremists and therefore that justifies the crimes. The Defence raised -- suggested that Slobodan Milosevic was supporting Milan Martic in the presidential election in the RSK at the end of 1993, beginning of 1994, merely to oppose Milan Babic and because of his opposition to UNPROFOR. What's harder to understand, however, is why Milan Martic was welcoming the support of Slobodan Milosevic, and that's the issue, is that he was embracing Slobodan Milosevic. The issue is not why Slobodan Milosevic supported Martic; it's why Milan Martic embraced Slobodan Milosevic. And I would point the Trial Chamber to Exhibits 13 and 14, a speech given by Milan Martic during the presidential campaign, where he described President Milosevic as "our all-Serbian leader" and pledged that if he were to win, he would pass on the baton to our all-Serbian leader, Slobodan Milosevic. Therefore, this connection between Slobodan Milosevic and Milan Martic at that time, in fact, supports the joint criminal enterprise allegations in the indictment. The Defence alleged that Milan Martic supported agreements with Croatia in March of 1994 and again -- this was a cease-fire agreement, and again in November of 1994, an economic agreement. This is ignoring all the other evidence in the trial. The evidence from Ambassador Galbraith is that the Serb side dragged its feet before they reached any kinds of agreements, in particular the November 1994 agreement. The evidence is also that Milan Martic specifically rejected the Z-4 -- the final Z-4 plan in January of 1995, and that evidence comes from Dzakula and also from Ambassador Galbraith, Dzakula at 441. I don't have a specific cite for Ambassador Galbraith, but I'm pretty sure I'm accurately recounting his testimony. The Defence has suggested that in fact Slobodan Milosevic supported the Z-4 plan; however, one of the principal negotiators, Ambassador Galbraith who testified, here suggested just the contrary. At this stage again, it's whether there is some evidence. The Trial Chamber doesn't need to resolve all of these disputes; it's just whether there is some evidence. But the suggestion I'm making is that the Defence in raising all these points has ignored all of the contrary evidence, all that is on the record. Again, there were a number of points raised about Croat aggressions during the years 1993 and 1994, 1995; those points I will not respond to. The point was made, and this is a point that's been made frequently through cross-examination, that the JNA was deployed on its own state, that the JNA was the army of the former Yugoslavia operating within the former Yugoslavia. Fine. But that does not really advance the ball at all because there is really no dispute about that. The -- that does not authorise the commission of war crimes. That does not authorise the joining up in a joint criminal enterprise with the purpose of creating the greater Serbia through the commission of crimes. So that point which has been made repeatedly really, in our submission, is besides the point. The point was also made that the -- all of the JNA troops and facilities were blocked and put in danger. That is -- first of all that's factually incorrect. MM-080 testified to the contrary. Secondly, there is evidence on the record that this was done for defensive reasons, that the Croats were merely trying to defend themselves from the JNA operating on the ground and trying to predetermine the situation with respect to Croatian independence, which was the -- one of the issues at the time and that evidence is at -- comes from Milan Babic, it's at 1562, 1563. And the third point to make about this, once again of course is that even to the extent there were blockades of JNA barracks, those are military actions that do not justify the commission of war crimes or crimes against humanity in response. The Defence did make some points with respect to some of the crime sites which I will respond to though, again, the Defence ignored all of the other evidence with respect to all of these crime sites. The first point with respect to -- I've just gotten a little piece of paper that says "break" on it. Maybe this would be a convenient time, since I'm just about to start in on this new topic of talking about the specific crime bases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before the break, I was starting to address the -- some of the points raised by Defence counsel with respect to specific crime bases, and the first one was with respect to Skabrnja. Defence counsel made much of the fact that there was some evidence about an independent battalion within Skabrnja. There are several responses. The first is that there is evidence that this was a -- that this was purely defensive. I'd refer the Trial Chamber to 2863 of Marko Miljanic's testimony, which Defence counsel I would note, relied on. The second is that the crimes -- the evidence is that the crimes committed at Skabrnja were committed against civilians while they were detained. So the -- whether there was an independent battalion or any other kind of a battalion there was completely irrelevant to those sorts of crimes. And there I would refer the Trial Chamber to the evidence of Neven Segaric, among others. The third point is that there is evidence on the record that the plan for the attack on Skabrnja had been made the night before; that comes from MM-080. And also, the Defence relied on MM-080 with regard to whether there was a -- whether there was information about an independent battalion being present in Skabrnja, but MM-080 of course also provided evidence, which I will not go into detail about, about information about crimes committed there, showing -- at Skabrnja, showing how the two are entirely consistent. And it should be noted that the information about crimes being committed at Skabrnja came, in part, from soldiers who were there who were appalled by what they saw, shocked, and reported it. However, the evidence is that nothing was ever done about them. The second area that was addressed was Bruska, and there, there is -- Defence counsel made a lot of the fact that this had been investigated and that nobody could be found. And we can't figure out who assassinated JFK, so how can we figure out this crime? The first point is that there is very strong evidence that -- overwhelming I would say, that these crimes, the crimes in Bruska, were committed by Martic's Police, men who were directly under the command of the accused. So that before the Trial Chamber even reaches the issue of punishment, it's why these men were committing these crimes in the first place, these men who were under his command, committing these crimes. The second is that Exhibit 404 is a report from 1992 which indicates that -- which provides evidence that the police knew who had committed the crimes and the suggestion in that report of -- that there was an effort to hide it, hide that fact and hide that information and cover it up. The third point we would make, certainly at this stage and no doubt ultimately, is that whatever investigation was done into the crimes in Bruska was clearly inadequate, clearly no real effort to determine the perpetrators and bring them to justice. These were -- these crimes were committed by the police; should not be that hard to figure out who had committed them. And the -- for the attitude of the accused towards punishment of individuals who have committed crimes, we would refer the Trial Chamber to the testimony of Mr. Van Lynden, the journalist who witnessed Mr. Martic release men who had been charged or who had been accused, let's say, not charged, but accused, by Captain Dragan in the summer of 1991 of having committed crimes in Struga. So certainly we think at this stage there is a sufficient basis to preserve the charges as they relate to Bruska, particularly since they -- as I said, they were committed by -- they were directly committed by Martic's Police, according to the evidence. The third area is Saborsko and Poljanak, and again the same claim is made that there were forces in Saborsko. And Defence even claiming that these -- the Croats who were defending themselves had turned their peaceful village into military barracks. There is evidence that these -- that these -- I don't even know what to call them, that the men in Saborsko were acting in a purely defensive manner, trying to protect themselves from attacks by Serbs, and that's at transcript 2662. It's corroborated by MM-037, who said that during the attack on Saborsko there was very little resistance and, to his knowledge, the Serb side did not suffer any casualties. The third point is that we would refer the Trial Chamber to, again, to the manner in which civilians were killed and the age of the civilians. And I'd refer the Trial Chamber specifically on this point to 2676 and to 77. Finally with respect to Poljanak and Lipovaca the same claim was made about a village guard. The evidence is that whatever village guard existed in those villages was purely defensive, and that's at 2413 to 14. Again, the presence of -- the attempt by the civilians of these villages to protect themselves, in some small way, does not justify in any way the crimes that were committed in those villages. The next point that the Defence makes is that these crimes were done by irresponsible individuals and by locals. Well, there are several points to make on this. The first is that the Martic's Police were of course comprised of locals. The second point is that the evidence shows with respect to all of the attacks on the villages named in the indictment, that they were organised operations, planned beforehand, that they included the participation of the TO, the JNA, Martic's Police. These were not just crimes of opportunity or isolated, individual crimes; these were crimes that were well-planned and committed in connection with well-planned military operations. The third point is that the evidence will show with respect to each crime base in the indictment, that the police, under the command of Milan Martic, participated in the attack on the village. And in our view, that is sufficient, certainly at this stage and, we believe, ultimately to hold the accused responsible under the joint criminal enterprise and other modes of liability. And finally, the -- there is evidence that the goal of these operations, both from statements made at the time and testimony from witnesses, but also from what happened in those villages, that the goal was plainly to wipe out those villages, to push out the Croat population, to destroy the village, and make sure that they would never come back, and to seize those villages as part of Serb territory. Most of the time to connect up Serb villages. Most of the time these villages were in the way, and so in order to connect up Serb villages that stood beyond them and make them contiguous part of the SAO Krajina, these villages were attacked. The next area that was addressed by Defence counsel is Dubica and Cerovljani. I had trouble getting clear on what the exact point of Defence counsel was, but what is clear and I think was conceded by Defence counsel is that in those areas all Croat forces, all Croat resistance, was gone by September of 1991, and certainly by October 1991, when the massacre occurred in Bacin. And the -- as I will discuss later, when I address more directly this area, the evidence is that the police, the SAO Krajina Police, was present in Dubica and that area at the time and that they participated in the operation that resulted in the massacre. The Defence counsel next moved on to talk about Zagreb. I'm not going to address everything that Defence counsel said; I will address a few points. The first point was that Defence counsel asserted that the Prosecution expert, Mr. Poje, said that the attack and Zagreb was general artillery support for the troops in Western Slavonia, meaning the SAO Krajina -- or the RSK troops in Western Slavonia. Perhaps true but still illegal. It's illegal artillery support for those troops, which brings me to the second that he raised which is -- he said: Well, this attack on Zagreb brought the aggression in Western Slavonia to a halt. I'm not sure that's true. I would dispute that. I think there were other reasons that the Operation Flash finished, namely that it was successful and completed. But even if true -- even if that were true, that is simply no justification for the illegal nature of the attack. A terrorist action which has results does not suddenly become lawful. The third point Defence counsel made was to suggest that the only weapons that the RSK had that would reach Zagreb, were these weapons, and that in fact Mr. Martic chose the better of the two options that he had. Again, this does not change whether that was a lawful action, and Mr. Poje himself addressed this point and said: If you don't have the lawful weapon to do the attack, then don't do the attack. The final point is that Defence counsel asserted that there were military targets in Zagreb. The evidence, in our view, shows - certainly at this stage and we think it will show ultimately - that the -- that this -- that the attack on Zagreb was never aimed at military targets. That's a post-event justification for the attack. The evidence is, in our view, clear that the -- that it was an attack aimed at civilians, at the civilians in Zagreb, and civilians in other cities. Even if -- and there is certainly evidence to support that on the record. Even if it were found that it was aimed at military targets, the evidence is that it was a wholly inappropriate and illegal weapon to choose with which to attack those targets because of the certainty of collateral damage, of civilians being murdered. Defence counsel made a final -- some final points about Martic's Police, for example, and whether we had invented that term. I think the evidence is quite clear that that was a term -- many, many witnesses testified that that was a term that was used by the police. I would refer the Trial Chamber to 2743, 2939, and in particular to the testimony of MM-078 at 4435, where he said that the members of Martic's Police bragged about being Martic's Police. So it's not a term that we came up with; it's a term that Martic's Police came up with. Finally, Defence counsel ended with an attack on a number of Prosecution witnesses. Those attacks -- I'm to the going to address them because they are inappropriate at this stage. The Trial Chamber is not, at this stage, supposed to weigh those sorts of issues, about credibility and so forth. That will come at a later stage. The -- however, I will say that many of -- much of what Defence counsel said about the witnesses and why they cannot be relied on is completely false. And I would particularly take a moment to say with respect to Mr. Babic that Defence counsel has selected a few words from the Parker report to suggest that Mr. Babic was -- first of all that it was clear that he would commit suicide and that he was emotionally unbalanced. Ignoring the fact that the Parker report, once it weighed out all the evidence and considered everything, came to the opposite conclusion on both of those points. Now, those are all my responses to the points raised by Defence counsel. What I would propose to do now is to just go through and indicate how we believe the -- there is evidence for all of the counts in the indictment. I will not go element by element; I'll spare the Trial Chamber that. However, if there is a particular element that, again, causes any concern, I'm happy to address it because I think we can. But I'll first talk about the joint criminal enterprise, and then I'd like to go through the different crime bases in the indictment. As I alluded to earlier, the elements of the joint criminal enterprise have been recently articulated by the Appeals Chamber in the Stakic appeals decision. And the elements are: Number 1, a plurality of persons -- I said I wasn't going to talk about elements, but only on this one I will. A common purpose which involves the commission of a crime and the participation of the accused. What's notable is that it does not require a plan, and the Stakic Appeals Chamber said with respect to common purpose that there is no need for the common purpose to have been previously arranged or formulated; rather, it may materialise extemporaneously and it may be inferred from the facts. There are -- under jurisprudence of the Tribunal, there are three types of joint criminal enterprise and the indictment in this case alleges, in the alternative, two of those types. It alleges first the first option -- the first option is that all of the crimes in the indictment were within the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise, and that is what's referred to in the jurisprudence as JCE 1. That there was a -- that all of the crimes were within the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. The second option which is alleged, the alternative charge in the indictment, is that counts 10 and 11, "... deportations or forcible transfers of Croat ... and other non-Serb ... from the SAO Krajina," was the object or purpose, common purpose, of the joint criminal enterprise. And that all of the other crimes were the natural and foreseeable consequence of the execution of that object of the JCE and that the accused was aware that such crimes were the possible outcome. That's what is commonly referred to as JCE 3. Now, what evidence is there of the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise, which in the indictment is alleged to be the forcible removal of non-Serbs from the Serb areas of Croatia, the SAO Krajina, and parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in order to make them part of a Serb-dominated state through the commission of crimes. That's the common -- that is the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise which is alleged in the indictment. And what evidence is there of that? Well, there are two parts to that. One is the greater -- the greater Serbia, creating a greater Serbia, and the second part is to do so through -- is to eliminate all non-Serbs from that greater Serbia through the commission of crimes. There are a number of ways that the evidence shows the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. The first is that -- the first is that witnesses have testified about -- directly, about the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. And I would suggest, and the -- and I think that the jurisprudence would suggest that this is actually kind of unusual to have witnesses who directly say what this was the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. Of course, not using that word, "joint criminal enterprise," but this was the purpose of what Serb forces -- this is what the Serb forces were doing. This was their purpose. Most of the time it's inferred from the facts, and I think it can be in this case, but we do have witnesses who directly testify about that. The first who does so of course is Milan Babic, and he testified -- he testified that he himself, at 1335, allowed himself to take part in persecutions of people simply because they were Croats and that innocent people were persecuted, that innocent people were forcibly evicted from their houses, and innocent people were killed. The -- his plea agreement and what he pled guilty to and what he admitted to as a factual basis for his plea of guilty, which was accepted by the Trial Chamber in his case is in evidence as Exhibit 174. And I would refer the Trial Chamber specifically to paragraphs 28 to 34 of tab 1 of the factual statement -- of tab 1, which is the factual statement, the factual basis for the guilty plea, where he takes responsibility for what happened. And there he describes the existence of the joint criminal enterprise, the purpose, and what it did. I won't go through all of the evidence that Milan Babic talked about, but he talked about in his testimony here, at 1384 and 1385, that starting in the fall of 1990 the Council for National Resistance, which the accused Milan Martic was in charge of - and that evidence is supported by Babic and others - it furthered the policy of Milosevic and Jovic and the policy he described as: "The policy of creation of a state to encompass all of the Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina as well by taking over Serb territories and for the others to leave Yugoslavia if they chose to." That was the essence of their policy. In the testimony of Milan Babic, he explained, and I won't quote from it, but he explained the -- what he described as the covert strategy and the public strategy of the joint criminal enterprise of Milan -- of Milosevic and others that was endorsed by the other members of the joint criminal enterprise, which was to publicly act in a passive way. We are protecting the former Yugoslavia, we are just trying to protect the system that existed, but covertly, at 1416, Babic said: "The covert strategy, however, was paramilitary forces, first in Croatia and then elsewhere, then to provoke incidents and try to include the JNA into the events, first to separate the warring parties and then to deploy the JNA in those territories that were envisaged as the future Serb state until later on retain the de facto situation that was supposed to have been recognised at a later stage by the international community." There is corroboration for this public -- this public/covert strategy in some intercepts, and I would refer the Trial Chamber specifically to Exhibit 200, 201, and 202, intercepts where the participants are clearly talking about what should be said publicly about the Serb strategy and what should be -- what in fact it was. There was also corroboration in the -- in Exhibit 476, which is the book by Borislav Jovic, one of the members of the joint criminal enterprise, and I'd specifically refer the Trial Chamber to the entries for the 23rd of June, 1989; the 27th of June, 1990; and the 11th of September 1990. Very early entries which show what the public and covert strategy were. This evidence about the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise didn't just come from Milan Babic; it came from others as well. Specifically, MM-003 testified that -- at 1981 to 1982, that in January 1991 the police were seeking a way as -- a way to the territories that were outside the barricades. A way was sought through the police stations that were closest to those places that did not belong to the SAO Krajina yet or had -- rather, had not become part of the Serb Krajina, the Serb territories yet. And at 2022 to 2023, Witness MM-003 described the relationship between the police and the JNA in this way -- and this is quite stark. "As I saw it, and as far as I know, it was excellent, more than excellent. In fact, they were on a joint assignment, I would say, it was a joint cooperation and a joint task, joint assignment for joining up all the Serb lands into one entity, one whole. "What would happen to Croat villages that were in the way? "Those, well, those villages were to be cleansed, quite simply, because they were in the way, towards opening communications, towards Serb territory. And as I understood it along certain axes, directions the direction to Lika, for example, the entire line was to be moved towards Gospic up to Gospic so you had pure villages." That is a very clear statement about the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. At 2023: "That meant that the Croatian population should either leave under these actions or, just simply, that they should be there no longer, to leave the territory, to leave those villages." There is further corroboration for the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise from Witness Dzakula at 404, where he said that: "Martic believed that we were supposed to work for recognition and joining the association of Serb lands, Republika Srpska and Serbia. Those were his landmarks." And MM-079 testified at 3069 to 70 that: "Martic said that the Serb people had expressed their readiness and willingness not to live in Croatia , and they were united in this demand that they wanted instead to live within Yugoslavia, that the Serbs of Krajina wanted to live in one single country with all the other Serbs from Yugoslavia, including Serbia." The -- those are explicit statements coming from witnesses about the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise, but the purpose can also be seen from the pattern of events that occurred starting really with the barricades in August of 1990, but continuing through 1991 and through the events that are charged in the indictment in the fall of 1991. And the -- as I said the pattern begins with the barricades. The -- Milan Babic testified at 1360 that the barricades on the -- that were erected beginning 17 August 1990 were the first step, the first time the Serbs -- the first use of force is what he said and -- by the Serb side. And MM-078 described how the -- I believe it's at 4418, that: "The barricades were not defensive. They had no other purpose than to psychologically intimidate citizens of both ethnicities," and he explained how they were directed against Croats. And MM-003 testified at 1968 to 1970 that the barricades cut off certain Croatian villages. The general pattern was described both by Milan Babic and Witness MM-078. Milan Babic described the pattern at 1418. He said that: "Their activities began in April 1991. At first they promoted discriminatory policies against Croats, only Croatian houses were searched and only Croatians were searched for weapons; then they were provoking in areas in contact with the Croatian settlements and areas, in particular the settlements controlled by the Republic of Croatia. They tried to provoke incidents and bring the JNA into the events." And then MM-078 at 4461, says: "I have to tell you there was a constant pressure on the Croatian citizens of Knin. This started in the year 1990," and he describes the ways that this pressure occurred. Now, the first -- or one of the first attacks on a village occurred in Potkonje, both Milan Babic and Witness MM-078 and, less directly, MM-079 testified about this. Babic testified at 1419. Witness MM-078 described at 4452 how Potkonje was attacked sometime before June of 1991 and it was done by the police under Martic's command. And the witness testified that -- this is a Croatian village of course, and that they wreaked havoc there and that the psychological effects were devastating, that the civilians left, and that the witness supposed that those who organised the attack had given careful thought to what the effect would be in Potkonje. This was the beginning of a series of attacks on villages with the same pattern, again and again and again. MM-079 testified about how sometime in June of 1991, some -- at least 600 refugees turned -- from the Knin area turned up in Sibenik, Croat civilians who had been driven away from the Knin area - Potkonje, of course, is very close to the Knin, it's part of the Knin area - and that they recounted how they had been driven away by Martic's Police, torching houses, beating people, telling them to leave. They were fleeing the crimes of Martic's Police. And the witness had a conversation with Milan Martic about these events; that's at 3112 to 13. And Milan Martic acknowledged being aware of them and defended what had occurred in various ways. And -- however, suggesting that the people who had any evidence of beatings had no doubt done it to themselves. But he did admit to torching of houses but defended it as being proper and appropriate. The next attack occurred at Lovinac, and this -- Babic testified about this at 1432 and 1433. And there is also evidence from MM-003 about this, which corroborates and in fact goes further, at 2010 and 2012 and also 2019. And the attack occurred around the June of 1991, again a Croat village. And MM-003 said the -- that: "Martic was in command of the attack and that the effect and the object of the attack was to drive the Croatian population out. They were -- they were in a panic. They wanted to leave, to escape, and that was the object of the attack, in fact." And then there was some further discussion about how he knew that, and at 2019 he said that "Martic talked about it, not just then but on other occasions." They did not -- they did talk about not only -- only about that day about the object of the attack, they were speaking generally. And they said they had to because of the large number of Serb population, they had to solve it beyond Letka [phoen]. The next event is in Struga and Glina in July 1991. There occurred -- Witness Van Lynden testified about that at 4995 to 5.000, and he described this as a very -- as an early attempt at ethnic cleansing. And as you'll recall, the attack on Struga is done by Territorial Defence -- what he thinks are Territorial Defence forces. During the attack on Struga, they murder some four to five women from Struga, ten Serb men are held by Captain Dragan, and Milan Martic releases them. Captain Dragan is also involved in the attack on Glina which is captured from the Croats. The next attack occurs in Kijevo; that is in August of 1991. And there again, Martic -- Martic's Police, participates with -- along with the TO and the JNA, and that's on the 26th of August, 1991. And there is evidence from Babic, from MM-003, MM-078, about the effect and the purpose of that attack, and the fact that the church was targeted and why it was targeted, and why the houses were torched, to send a message to the Croats living there that there was no reason to return. Kijevo is followed by Vrljika, MM-078 talks about that; followed by Drnis, MM-078 talks about that, again police involved. Again the same pattern of destroying the villages, driving out the Croats, and looting and plundering, all with the participation of the police. And then we reach the crimes charged in the indictment, and I'll go through those in a moment, but there is also evidence which comes just still on the point of the joint criminal enterprise, that the -- which shows that all during 1991, Martic's -- Martic and the forces under him, Martic's Police and during a period also the Territorial Defence forces, from mid-August to the end of September 1991, along with the TO and the JNA, were all cooperating and working together. The -- Milan Babic described this as a parallel structure, the cooperation between the forces around Milan Martic in the SAO Krajina and the forces in Serbia that -- whether they be the JNA, the Ministry of the Defence, or the Minister of the Interior, and he talked about that at 1567. This is corroborated by MM-003 who talked about -- at 1994, about how Martic began receiving -- and in other places, how Martic very early on in -- beginning in 1990 and continuing through 1991, how Martic began receiving support from Serbia, from Milosevic, from Stanisic, from Simatovic. This -- it's also corroborated by MM-079 and by Witness Maksic. This culminates, of course, in the creation of the Golubic camp in April of 1991, where a camp which is financed by Serbia, by Stanisic, by Simatovic, through the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, and where Martic's special units, his police, are trained for the purpose of engaging in military action. And the evidence about Golubic comes from Babic at 1397 and 1539, but from many other witnesses as well: MM-003, MM-078, MM-079. By the fall of 1991 -- by Kijevo -- the attack on Kijevo marks the time when the JNA enters, gives up this role of acting as a buffer between the parties and begins actively engaging in the conflict, and from the attack on Kijevo thereafter, the evidence -- there is evidence, substantial evidence, that the JNA, the TO, and the police worked together during the fall of 1991, that they were fully coordinated. This comes from Babic at 1438, and in particular at 1447 to 1448, where he said that: "There was an essential change in fact, the JNA became an active participant in the war, the JNA went to war, and under such conditions all TO units automatically came under the command of the JNA." It is corroborated by Exhibits 213 to 215, which are articles where Milan Martic openly - openly - in many different newspapers talks about the good cooperation and close coordination between the army and the police, and it's corroborated also by Dzakula at page 424; by Exhibit 518, a speech by Milan Martic in December of 1991, where he talks about the police coordinating with the TO and the JNA; and it's also corroborated by MM-078 at 4426; MM-078 at 4442. By the time of Kijevo and thereafter, all of the Serb forces, the JNA, the TO, and the police, were working together for the common purpose of the JCE that's alleged in the indictment. So what was the result? The result was the crimes alleged in the indictment, and I'll go through them now as briefly as I can, one by one. We will start -- I'll do it chronologically. I'm going to leave -- I won't -- I'm going to go through the different crime bases because they, I think by the end, establish the facts for all of the different counts in the indictment. The persecutions, murders, detentions, are a little bit separate, that's kind of a separate one, and the forcible transfer, as well as the destruction and plunder counts. The evidence -- the pattern continues with all of the crime -- the pattern that's established from Potkonje through all the different events that occur, continues where -- it begins. There is shelling, barricades set up, there is shelling of the village, followed by an attack on the village - these are all Croat villages of course - attack on the village, murders occur, the civilians are driven out, and the village is completely destroyed and plundered and looted. And in each case, the police participate in the attack on the village. And it's the same pattern again and again and again in each case. Start with Dubica. The evidence -- the massacre occurs on the 20th or 21st of October, 1991. The evidence, however, is that Dubica and the villages around Dubica, Cerovljani and Bacin, were attacked by shelling and by Serb forces in August and September of 1991, and that already by September of 1991, the Serb forces - and in particular Martic's Police - controlled these areas, controlled these villages. And the evidence comes from Witness Kozarcanin and that's Exhibit 828, he's a 92 bis witness; Witness MM-022, Witness Ana Kesic; Witness Mijo Cipric. Ana Kesic said that by September of 1991 most of the Croats living in the village of Dubica had left, had been driven out, and only the elderly people remained. Witness Mijo Cipric testified that when the Serbs started shelling the area in August of 1991, the Croats had no option but to leave their villages. The -- several witnesses talk about the events of October 20th and 21st that lead up to the massacre that occurred in Bacin and Cerovljani, Dubica. The individuals being taken to the fire station, and in particular Witness MM-022 was able to identify with great specificity a list of individuals who were left in the fire station that day and who later were exhumed from a mass grave in Bacin. The evidence is -- there is evidence which shows that the SAO Krajina Police participated in these events that led to the massacre. First of all, as I said before, they were -- in October of 1991, they were present and operating in Dubica and that comes from MM-022, at 2289; and also from Witness Josip Josipovic at 3353. The -- MM-022 talked about the involvement of a truck with the inscription of the SAO Krajina Police on it in -- bringing people to the fire station who were ultimately murdered. This witness says that the police -- this witness who knew that the Dubica -- and knew the situation there and who controlled Dubica, said that the police, and that specifically Stevo Radunovic -- or sorry, Veljo Radunovic, one of the commanders of the police, would have to know why those people had been collected, and in fact, he tried to get in touch with Veljo Radunovic at that time, and the reference there is 2314. The witness Ana Kesic, who testified that Veljo Radunovic who has been identified as one of the commanders of the SAO Krajina Police as one of the people who took her and others to the fire station, and Witness Kozarcanin, again Exhibit 828, said that someone by the name of Stevo Radjun, which is a name that was used for Stevo Radunovic, one of the commanders of the SAO Krajina Police, was guarding the fire station. MM-022 talked about later encounters with the police which I will not go into further detail on, so as not to identify him, but they further suggest police involvement and police knowledge of the massacre in Bacin. Of course, Josip Josipovic, who was arrested and detained prior to the massacre and who suffered horrific conditions and treatment in Dubica, testified that the police -- that it was -- he was detained at the hands of the police and he identified a patch of the Milicija Krajina - it's Exhibit 266 - which incidentally in some videos which have been admitted into evidence we see the accused Milan Martic also wearing on his sleeve in the fall of 1991. When -- I'm -- Your Honour, I don't know if you have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead. If I do, you will know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The witnesses who all -- who have left these villages, Dubica, Cerovljani, and Bacin, all testified that when they returned, the villages were destroyed and churches in these villages had been destroyed. Witness Anton Blazevic said that actually this -- the Serbs in -- came to Cerovljani already in September of 1991 and burned down houses and that on the 24th of September, they targeted the Catholic church in that village. Kozarcanin testified -- or stated in his statement, that Serbs were involved in looting and burning of houses in Dubica; that when he returned in 1995, he found that many of the houses in Dubica were burnt down and plundered. Josip Josipovic testified that all of the Serbs forces, be it the JNA or the TO or the police, were involved in looting. This was further corroborated by Witness Mijo Cipric, Witness MM-022, who specifically stated that the police engaged in looting, and Witness Ana Kesic. It's also corroborated by Witness Charles Kirudja, who confirmed that whenever they drove to Sector North he saw that villages that had been previously occupied by Croats had been destroyed. And this destruction included the churches specifically; That comes from several witnesses. These -- all of these witnesses: Blazevic, Kozarcanin, Josipovic, Cipric, MM-025, another protected witness, testified that the -- that the Croat civilians were driven out of the area by these attacks by Serbs and of course by the massacre. Milan Babic testified that when he was in Kostajnica -- he was in Dubica in 1993, and he saw that many of the settlements where Croats had lived were destroyed that there were no Croats left. So that is Dubica, Cerovljani, Bacin, and it covers I think the murder, forcible transfer counts, and the plunder and destruction counts. Going to -- now to Saborsko, Poljanak, and Vukovici, and Lipovaca, again, the evidence shows that Saborsko was shelled in the summer of 1991 as early as June or July of 1991, and certainly by August of 1991; and that evidence comes from Marica Vukovic at 2412, and Marko and Vlado Vukovic at 2574 to 2579 and 2658. Ana Bicanic, in her 92 bis statement said that the shooting of by the Serbs at Saborsko was mainly at the school and the church and that this shelling intensified after the 5th of August, 1991. There was shelling nearly every day, and that many buildings were damaged, including the church. That comes from Vlado Vukovic at 2659. The attack, the main attack on Saborsko, occurred on the 12th of November, 1991, and the evidence from MM-037 and from other sources, which I'll discuss in a moment, is that Martic's Police participated in the attack, both the regular police and the special police participated in the attack on Saborsko. The evidence from Ana Bicanic and from Jure Vukovic is that during the attack, houses were burned down and that civilians who had surrendered were separated, the men from the women, and that the men were shot and killed while the women and children were told to flee, and that some -- Jure Vukovic says that one person, Djakju [phoen] Vukovic was shot while fleeing. Vlado Vukovic testified that the people who were killed in Saborsko included women and very old people. I believe one man was 100 years old. The result of the attack on Saborsko was complete destruction of the village. The entire village was destroyed, according to Marko Vukovic and Vlado Vukovic, including the church. When Jure Vukovic returned to Saborsko after Operation Storm, the entire village was destroyed. There were no houses, and the churches -- the main church was rubble while the smaller church was heavily damaged, and this is corroborated by -- also by Ana Bicanic, who found the same thing when she returned to Saborsko. The same pattern occurred in Poljanak, Vukovici. In August of 1991, Poljanak started to be shelled, and civilians there started to leave their houses and sometimes sleep in the woods. And just before the attack on Saborsko, Vukovici and Poljanak were attacked. They were attacked on the 7th of November which was three days before the planned attack on Saborsko, which was supposed to occur on the 10th of November but which did not occur until the 12th of November. And the evidence from Marija -- Marica Vukovic and MM-038 is about the murders and complete destruction that occurred in Poljanak and Vukovici. And the evidence from witness MM-037 is that these -- all of these villages were attacked at around the same time with the purpose of linking up the Serb area of Plaski with the SAO Krajina and that these villages stood in the way of that. The evidence for the attack on Lipovaca comes from MM-036. Again, the JNA started rocket attacks against Lipovaca in August of 1991, and in October of 1991 the JNA entered Lipovaca and almost all the villagers fled with only, again, elderly people staying behind. And according to the evidence, in early -- in October, on the 28th of October, 1991, the victims in Lipovaca were murdered, and that is according to Exhibit 323, MM-036, and Ivan Marjanovic. When MM-036 returned to Lipovaca in 1995, it was totally destroyed, looted, burned, completely destroyed. As I said before, there is evidence from MM-037 about the participation of Martic's Police in these operations, which in Saborsko -- he speaks specifically about Saborsko, and I would also refer the Trial Chamber to Exhibit 607, Exhibit 603, and Exhibit 605, which also talk about the participation of the -- of SAO Krajina Police in these -- in the operation on Saborsko. And again, the evidence is that the other village -- that all these villages were attacked really as part of one operation. I would also refer the Trial Chamber to Exhibit 507, which is a statement taken by the Croatian MUP in April of 1994 from a witness who said that a member of Martic's Police claimed to have shot eight people during the attack on Saborsko because he hated all Ustashas, and that the commander of the Martic's Police instructed him and others how to behave during the attack, including that there should be a maximum of 30 people killed, and that the police boasted about setting houses on fire, robbing houses, stealing vehicles, tractors, and livestock. Milan Babic also testified about the attack in this area and the -- the area north of Plitvica in November of 1991 and the resulting expulsion of Croat civilians from the area and the Serb takeover, which is entirely consistent with all of the victims who testified about the attacks on that area, and that's at 1582. In -- with respect to all these villages, the victims have been identified specifically by, in the testimony of Mr. Strinovic and Mr. Grujic. There is also specific evidence about cause of death in many of the cases, many cases of gun-shot wounds, many cases gun-shot wounds at close range. That's particularly relevant for places like Saborsko. Many of the victims were killed not by shelling or, you know, explosions but were killed by gun-shot wounds, oftentimes at close range. There is specific evidence about plunder, looting, with respect to Saborsko that comes from MM-037, at page 3 of Exhibit 268. Now, moving on to the attack on Skabrnja and Nadin -- well, Skabrnja and Nadin I'll take together. The evidence again is that from Marko Miljanic is that there was shelling of Skabrnja, and then Marko Miljanic and in particular Neven Segaric provide evidence about the crimes committed at Skabrnja. He testified that Josip Miljanic and another neighbour, Stana Vikovic both -- one 60 years old and one 50 years old, were forced to kneel down. And a soldier wearing a camouflage uniform with an SAO Krajina, on his shoulder, patch then shot them both in the head, killing them. There was no warning before -- there is evidence that there was no warning before the attack and that there was no provocation before the attack, and that is at 2835 and at 2868. Again, Witnesses Grujic and Strinovic talk about the bodies of the victims, with respect to the later -- the indictment charges, really two attacks on Skabrnja. Paragraph 31 charges an attack on the 18th of November with specific victims; paragraph 33 charges a continuing attack between the 18th of November through February 1992, where additional killings occurred. And that second allegation is supported by Witness Bosko Brkic, by Witness Miljanic at 2877, and also by Mr. Strinovic. There is evidence that Martic's forces -- once again, Martic's Police, participated in this attack. MM-003 testified about how Martic spoke with pride about Skabrnja and that he talked specifically about Goran Opacic, and this person provides one specific link to Milan Martic. To MM-003's knowledge, Goran Opacic was under Martic's command at this -- at the time the operation was carried out, that he was a member of the Benkovac special police. Milan Babic testified that Opacic was subordinated to and close to Martic, and that he learned from another person Opacic was there at the outset of the fighting. That's corroborated -- his being there during the fighting was corroborated -- is corroborated by Exhibit 411, which also identifies him as being a member of the police. There is contrary evidence that he was a member of the TO at that time; however, I don't think that's an issue that the Trial Chamber has to resolve at this point. There is evidence that he was a member of the police. There is also evidence of close cooperation -- from Exhibit 107, there is evidence of close cooperation between the TO and the police in the attack on Skabrnja. There is even a reference to the TO loaning a unit to the police just before the attack. There is evidence from Exhibit 614 that Bosko Drazic, who was the commander of the police in Benkovac, was present during the attack, and in fact the evidence from that exhibit suggests that he failed to protect a civilian who had been confronted by the TO, but it certainly establishes that he's present. And Exhibit 107, which is the notes of the commander of the attack, Lieutenant Bugunovic, also show that is with respect to both Nadin and Skabrnja, which were a joint operation, and that's made clear by the -- it's made clear by the dates of the attacks, they occur within one day of each other, their proximity, and also by this exhibit, Exhibit 107, which shows that they were planned together and executed together. And that exhibit also show that is Bosko Drazic was present during the attack, indicating that the police also took part in the attack on Skabrnja. As I noted before, there is evidence this attack had been planned, at least by the day before. It was not a spontaneous event or defensive action - the attack had been planned - and that comes from Witness MM-080. And then Bosko Brkic provides evidence that from the end of November 1991 until December 1992, Skabrnja was constantly looted and burned and that in the end it was completely destroyed. The evidence for the attack on Nadin of course comes from Witness MM-083. I don't think I need to recount what occurred, what that witness testified to; however, it's worth noting that again, that witness testified that there had been shelling, again following the same pattern, shelling, attack, murders, drive out the population, destroy the village, and that the shelling had occurred in September, on the 16th of September, and the 2nd of October of 1991, in advance of the attack which occurred on the 18th and 19th of November of 1991. And with Nadin as well the victims had been established by both Witnesses Grujic and Strinovic. We come then to the events in Bruska which occurred in December of 1991, and Witnesses Jasna Denona, and Ante Marinovic testified about what occurred in Bruska on the 21st of December, 1991, resulting in the murder of nine Croats and one Serb who had friendly relations with the Croat families. And the evidence shows that the perpetrators of that -- of those murders, were Martic's Police. Again, I would refer -- and this comes both from the way that the individuals identified themselves and also from the patch that Ante Marinovic identified on the sleeve of their uniforms. I would again refer the Trial Chamber to Exhibit 404, which indicates that the police knew who killed the people in Bruska, and that one police officer who knew the most about it had been transferred overnight to somewhere in Serbia, and that that had been done certainly with -- by someone with a top position in the MUP. Vaganac is -- it's alleged that Vaganac is one of the locations that was attacked and Marica Vukovic testified that it had been attacked and people were killed there and that there were no houses there --
